Handlebody diagram algebras
Daniel Tubbenhauer and Pedro Vaz

Abstract
. In this paper we study handlebody versions of some classical diagram algebras, most prominently, handlebody versions of Temperley–Lieb, blob, Brauer, BMW, Hecke and Ariki–Koike algebras. Moreover, motivated by Green–Kazhdan–Lusztig’s theory of cells, we reformulate the notion of (sandwich, inflated or affine) cellular algebras. We explain this reformulation and how all of the above algebras are part of this theory.

†
†

Mathematics Subject Classification 2020.
Primary: 16G99; Secondary: 18M30, 20C08, 20F36, 57K14.
†
†

Keywords.
Diagrammatic algebra, cellular algebras, braid groups, handlebodies.

1.
Introduction

A large collection of diagram algebras, such as Temperley–Lieb
or (type A) Hecke algebras, are interesting from at least two perspectives:
they are of fundamental importance in low-dimensional topology
and they also have a rich representation theory.

Having an eye on the study of links in
3-manifolds brings the topology of the ambient space into play.
In all the classical examples, like Temperley–Lieb or
Hecke algebras, the ambient space is the 3-ball, and these algebras
are related to spherical Coxeter groups and Artin–Tits braid groups.
In the simplest case beyond the 3-ball,
when one passes to links in a solid torus,
these diagram algebras get replaced by their (extended) affine versions,
and the related objects are now affine Coxeter groups and Artin–Tits braid groups.
A natural question is what kind of diagrammatics and Coxeter combinatorics
one could expect for more general 3-manifolds.

In this paper we consider (three-dimensional) handlebodies of genus
g
.
The 3-ball and the solid torus correspond to

g=0
(called classical in this paper) and
g=1
, respectively.
As we will see, the Temperley–Lieb and Hecke algebras, their
affine versions as well
as algebras along the same lines,
can be seen as a low genus class
of a more general, higher genus, class of diagram algebras.

In case
g=0
these diagram algebras and their associated
braid groups are around for donkey’s years.
For
g=1
there is a long history of work on this topic which
goes back to at least Brieskorn
[
Br73
]
.
For example (with more references to come later on), see

[
Al02
]
for braid pictures,
[
GL97
]
or
[
OR04
]
for connections
to knot theory,
[
Gr98
]

or
[
HO01b
]
for affine diagram algebras.
To the best of our knowledge, the first attempts to give a
description of braids in handlebodies are due to Vershinin
[
Ve98
]

and Häring-Oldenburg–Lambropoulou
[
La00
]
,
[
HOL02
]
,
while Lambropoulou studied links in 3-manifolds even before that
[
La93
]
.

From the representation theoretical point of view all these
algebras share the common feature of being cellular in a certain way
that we will make precise. In a nutshell, in the
g=0
case
these algebras are often cellular in the sense of Graham–Lehrer
[
GL96
]
,
and in the
g=1
case they are often affine cellular in the sense of König–Xi
[
KX12
]
.

We see this paper as a continuation of these works, focusing on the diagrammatic,
algebraic and representation theoretical aspects. That is, we generalize
some diagram algebras to higher genus, and
we show that they are sandwich cellular.
(Sandwich cellular is a notion that
generalizes cellularity. Roughly speaking it means that the original
algebra can be obtained by sandwiching smaller algebras.
One of the upshots of being sandwich cellular is that the
classification of simple modules is reduced
from the original algebra to the sandwiched algebras.)

1A.
What this paper does

Our starting point is a diagrammatic description of
handlebody braid groups of genus
g
, i.e. a diagrammatic
description of the configuration space of a disk with

g
punctures. The pictures hereby are e.g.

the core strands correspond to cores of a
handlebody as explained in e.g.

[
RT21
, Section 2]
, hence the name. All links in such handlebodies can
be obtained by this closing procedure, and there is also an associated
Markov theorem. In other words, the handlebody braid group gives an
algebraic way to study links in handlebodies. The main references
here are
[
Ve98
]
and
[
HOL02
]
.
After explaining this setup more carefully, building upon the aforementioned
works, in
Section 3

we also study an associated handlebody Coxeter group for which we find a basis
using versions of Jucys–Murphy elements.

These handlebody braid pictures are also our starting point to define and study
various diagram algebras associated to handlebodies:

(a)

In
Section 4
we study handlebody Temperley–Lieb and blob algebras. The pictures to keep in mind are crossingless matchings
and core strands
(left, Temperley–Lieb)
respectively crossingless matchings decorated with colored blobs
(right, blob):

Note that the blobs illustrated in the right picture come in colors,
corresponding to the various cores strands. These algebras
generalize Temperley–Lieb algebras and blob algebras:
If
g=0
, then these two algebras are the same as the classical
Temperley–Lieb algebra.
For
g\geq 1
they are not the same anymore (at least
in our formulation), and have a long history of study
starting with e.g.
[
MS94
]
.

Section 5

As before, the case
g=0
is classical and goes back to Brauer, while

g=1
appears in
[
HO01a
]
.
In the same section we also study their cyclotomic quotients.

(c)

Finally,
Section 6
studies handlebody versions of Hecke and Ariki–Koike algebras.
The picture for handlebody Hecke algebras is the same as for handlebody braid groups,
while we choose to illustrate handlebody versions of Ariki–Koike algebras using blobs, e.g.

The cases
g=0
and
g=1
are, of course, well-studied and they correspond to
Hecke respectively extended affine Hecke algebras or cyclotomic quotients.
We learned about the
g>1
case from
[
La00
]

and
[
Ba17
]
.

We also study a generalization of cellularity in

Section 2
, giving us a toolkit to parameterize the simples
modules of the aforementioned algebras.
Note hereby that this generalization heavily builds on and borrows from
[
Gr51
]
,
[
KX99
]
,
[
GW15
]

or
[
ET21
]
.
Although it might be known to experts,
our exposition is new.

1B.
Speculations

Let us mention a number of possible future directions.

\bullet

Quantum topology.

A manifest direction which we do not explore in
this work would be to study these algebras
in connections to quantum topology and its ramifications.

For example, for
g=1

[
GL97
]
and
[
OR04
]

construct link invariants
from Markov traces, and
these link invariants admit categorifications
[
WW11
]
.
For
g>1

[
RT21
]
takes a few first steps towards
categorical handlebody link invariants,
but this direction appears to be widely open otherwise.

Moreover, for
g=0
most of these diagram algebras are related to
representation theory by some form of Schur–Weyl duality.
(In fact, this was the reason to define e.g. the Temperley–Lieb
algebras to begin with, see
[
RTW32
]
.)
Some work for higher genus on this representation theoretical
aspect is done,
e.g. in relation to Verma modules
[
ILZ21
]
,

[
LV21
]
,
[
DR18
]
or complex reflection groups
[
MS16
]
,
[
SS99
]
. Following this track for higher genus
seems to be a worthwhile goal.

\bullet

Diagram algebras.
There are plenty
of diagram algebras that we do not considered in this
paper, but for which (some version of) our discussion goes through.

Examples of such algebras that come to mind that appear in classical
literature are partition algebras
[
Ma91
]
,
rook monoid algebras
[
So90
]
, walled
Brauer algebras
[
Ko89
]
and alike.
Other examples are related to knot theory and categorification
such as (type A) webs appearing in a version
of Schur–Weyl duality
[
CKM14
]
,
[
RT16
]
,

[
QS19
]
,

[
TVW17
]
.

Diagrammatic algebras are also important in categorification.
After the introduction of the diagrammatic version of the
KLR algebra
[
KL09
]

(see also
[
Ro08
]
)
they have become quite popular, and might admit handlebody extensions.
For example, alongside with KLR algebras
Webster’s tensor product algebras
[
We17
]
,
algebras related to Verma categorifications

[
NV18
]
,
[
NV22
]
,
[
MV19
]
,
[
LNV20
]
, Soergel diagrammatics
[
EW14
]
,
potentially admit handlebody versions, just to name a few.

We also expect these handlebody diagram
algebras to have “nice” sandwich cellular bases.

\bullet

Categories instead of algebras.

All of our algebras and concepts under study also have appropriate
categorical versions.

For example, it should be fairly straightforward
to generalize our discussion of
Section 2

to cellular categories
[
We09
]
,

[
EL16
]
.
However, let us mention that a reason why we have not
touched upon categorical versions of our handlebody diagram
algebras is that these do not form monoidal categories
for
g>0
(at least not in any reasonable sense as far as we are aware), but
rather module categories. We think this deserves a thorough
treatment, following for example
[
HO01a
]

or
[
ST19
]
.

1C.
How to read this paper

Section 2
explains our generalization
of cellularity and is independent of the rest. It can be easily skipped
during a first reading.

Section 3

treats handlebody braid and Coxeter groups and
is fundamental for
all sections following it. Moreover, to avoid
too much repetition, we decided to construct the remaining sections
assuming the reader knows
Section 4
, in which we
define handlebody Temperley–Lieb and blob algebras. So
this section is mandatory if one wants to read either
Section 5
, the BMW part,
or
Section 6
, the Hecke part.

Acknowledgments.

We thank a referee, Abel Lacabanne, David Rose, Catharina Stroppel and Arik Wilbert for comments on this paper and discussions related
to the diagrammatics of handlebodies.

D.T. does not deserve to be supported, but was still supported
by the Hausdorff Research Institute for Mathematics (HIM)
during the Junior Trimester Program New Trends in Representation Theory.
Part of this paper were written during that program, which
is gratefully acknowledged.
P.V. was supported by the Fonds de la Recherche
Scientifique - FNRS under Grant no. MIS-F.4536.19.

2.
A generalization of cellularity

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a unital, commutative, Noetherian domain, e.g.
the integers or a field, or polynomial rings over these. Everything
in this paper is linear over
\mathbbm{K}
.
In particular, algebras are
\mathbbm{K}
-algebras.

2A.
Inflation by algebras

We start by defining sandwich cellular algebras.

Remark 2.0

Our discussion below is motivated by Green’s
theory of cells
[
Gr51
]
,
often called Green’s relations,
and the Clifford–Munn–Ponizovskiĭ theorem
(see e.g.
[
GMS09
]

for a modern formulation).
In fact, we have borrowed
part of the terminology from the literature on semigroups.

The following generalization of the notion
of cellularity from
[
GL96
]
is well-known
to experts, see e.g.
[
KX99
]

or
[
GW15
]
for
basis-free formulations.
Nevertheless, we will state this generalization and some consequences
of it.

Definition 2.0

A
sandwich cellular algebra
over

\mathbbm{K}
is an associative, unital algebra

\mathrm{A}
together with a
sandwich cellular datum
, that is:

\bullet

A partial ordered set
\Lambda=\text{(}\Lambda,\leq_{\Lambda}\text{)}
(we also write
<_{\Lambda}
etc. having the usual meaning);

\bullet

finite sets
M_{\lambda}
(bottom) and
N_{\lambda}
(top) for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
;

\bullet

an algebra
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
and a fixed basis
\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}
of it for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
;

\bullet

a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis
\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,D\in M_{\lambda},U\in N_{\lambda},b\in\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}\}
of
\mathrm{A}
;

such that we have

(a)

For all
x\in\mathrm{A}
there exist scalars

r(S,D)\in R
that do not depend
on
U
or on
b
, such that

(2-1)

\displaystyle xc_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\equiv\sum_{S\in M_{\lambda},a\in\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}}r(S,D)\cdot c_{S,a,U}^{\lambda}\pmod{\mathrm{A}^{<_{\Lambda}\lambda}},

where
\mathrm{A}^{<_{\Lambda}\lambda}
is the
\mathbbm{K}
-submodule of
\mathrm{A}
spanned by the set

\{c_{D,b,U}^{\mu}|\mu\in\Lambda,\mu<_{\Lambda}\lambda,D\in M_{\mu},U\in N_{\mu},b\in\mathrm{B}_{\mu}\}
. We also have a similar condition for right
multiplication.

(b)

Let
\mathrm{A}(\lambda)=\mathrm{A}^{\leq_{\Lambda}\lambda}/\mathrm{A}^{<_{\Lambda}\lambda}
, where

\mathrm{A}^{\leq_{\Lambda}\lambda}
is the
\mathbbm{K}
-submodule of
\mathrm{A}
spanned
by the set
\{c_{D,b,U}^{\mu}|\mu\in\Lambda,\mu\leq_{\Lambda}\lambda,D\in M_{\mu},U\in N_{\mu},b\in\mathrm{B}_{\mu}\}
.
Then
\mathrm{A}(\lambda)
is isomorphic to

\Delta(\lambda)\otimes_{\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}}(\lambda)\Delta
for free graded right and left

\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
-modules
\Delta(\lambda)
and
(\lambda)\Delta
, respectively.

The set
\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,D\in M_{\lambda},U\in N_{\lambda},b\in\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}\}

is called a
(sandwich) cellular basis
.

We very often have
M_{\lambda}=N_{\lambda}
, and we will then
omit
N_{\lambda}
from the notation. In particular, from
Section 2D

onward we always have
M_{\lambda}=N_{\lambda}
.

Remark 2.0

One of the advantages of the basis-focused formulation
above is that

Section 2A
works, mutatis mutandis, for relative
cellular algebras as in
[
ET21
]

or (strictly object-adapted) cellular
categories
[
We09
]
,
[
EL16
]
.

We also define:

Definition 2.0

A sandwich cellular algebra
\mathrm{A}
is called
involutive

if
M_{\lambda}=N_{\lambda}
for all
\lambda\in\Lambda

and
\mathrm{A}
admits an antiinvolution
({}_{-})^{\star}\colon\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{A}

compatible with the cell structure. That is,

({}_{-})^{\star}
restricts to
an antiinvolution
({}_{-})^{\star}\colon\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}\to\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
that is a bijection on
\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}

for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
, and we have

(2-2)

\displaystyle(c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda})^{\star}=c_{U,b^{\star},D}^{\lambda}.

Convention 2.0

We will use diagrammatics from now on.
Our reading conventions for diagrams are
summarized by

\displaystyle\hbox to48.71pt{\vbox to43.58pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 44.77708pt\lower-0.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}
{{{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}}{{{}}{{}}}{}{{}}{}{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -19.69 0 C -19.69 3.84 -19.69 6 -19.69 9.84}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}

The picture in (
2-3
) is an accurate description for all diagram algebras that we use in this paper. However, these pictures should be taken with care as the definition of a sandwich cellular datum is more general.

Throughout the rest of this section
we write
\mathrm{A}
for a sandwich cellular algebra
with a fixed sandwich cell datum, using the notation from

Section 2A
.
We will use the terminology of being a sandwich cellular algebra
in the sense that we have fixed a sandwich cell datum.
As we will see in e.g.
Theorem 2.7
, our focus
is indeed not on whether an algebra is sandwich cellular but rather
whether one can find a useful sandwich cell datum. Here is an explicit example
of a not very useful sandwich cell datum:

Example 2.0

For any group
\mathrm{G}
the group element basis
is a sandwich cellular basis in the sense of
Section 2A
.
To see this we let
\Lambda=\{\bullet\}=M_{\bullet}=N_{\bullet}
be trivial,
and set
c_{\bullet,b,\bullet}=b
for
b\in\mathrm{G}

seen as an element of
\mathbb{S}_{\bullet}=\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{G}
.
For this choice
Theorem 2.7

does not reduce the classification
problem of finding the simple
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{G}
-modules.

Example 2.0

For (important) special cases, the above has appeared in the literature.
If
\mathrm{A}
is involutive, then:

(a)

If
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}
for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
,
then the notion of a sandwich cell datum above is the same as
the classical one from
[
GL96
]
. Conversely, any cell datum in
the sense of
[
GL96
]
is a sandwich cell datum in the above sense
by letting
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}
for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
.

(b)

If
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}[X,X^{-1}]

for all
\lambda\in\Lambda
,
then a sandwich cellular algebras is affine cellular
as in
[
KX12
]
. Allowing
any quotient of a finite polynomial ring as
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
,
the converse is also true as one can check.

Having
Section 3
in mind,
we note that
\mathbbm{K}\cong\mathbbm{K}\big[\pi_{1}(D_{0})\big]

and
\mathbbm{K}[X,X^{-1}]\cong\mathbbm{K}\big[\pi_{1}(D_{1})\big]
,
where
\pi_{1}(D_{0})
respectively
\pi_{1}(D_{1})

are the fundamental groups of a disc

D_{0}
or a punctured disc
D_{1}
.

Example 2.0

The notion of being (involutive) sandwich cellular
is a strict generalization of
being cellular. An easy, albeit silly, example is to take

\Lambda=\{\bullet\}=M_{\bullet}=N_{\bullet}
and
\mathbb{S}_{\bullet}

to be a non-cellular algebra. As an explicit example
consider the set of upper triangular

2
x
2
matrices over
\mathbbm{K}
, and view it as a semigroup
so that
\{c_{\bullet,b_{i},\bullet}^{\bullet}=b_{i}\}_{i}

is the semigroup basis of the semigroup ring

\mathbb{S}_{\bullet}
.
See
[
ET21
]
for several examples of non-cellular algebras
which one could take as
\mathbb{S}_{\bullet}
.

The comparison of sandwich cellular to cellular algebras is:

Proposition 2.1

An involutive sandwich cellular algebra
\mathrm{A}

such that all
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
are cellular
(with the same antiinvolution
({}_{-})^{\star}
) is cellular
with a refined sandwich cell datum.
Conversely, if at least one
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
is non-cellular, then

\mathrm{A}
is non-cellular.

Note that an algebra can be sandwich cellular without the

\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
being cellular, cf.
Section 2A
.

Proof.

The trick is to use the sandwich cell datum of the

\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}

(let us fix any such datum compatible with

({}_{-})^{\star}
) to make
\Lambda
finer. The picture is

Precisely, we define

\Lambda^{\prime}=\{(\lambda,\mu)\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,\mu\in\Lambda_{\lambda}\}
with
\Lambda_{\lambda}

being the poset associated to
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
. The order on

\Lambda^{\prime}
is
(\lambda,\mu)\leq_{\Lambda^{\prime}}(\lambda^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})

if (
\lambda<_{\Lambda}\lambda^{\prime}
) or
(
\lambda=\lambda^{\prime}
and
\mu\leq_{\Lambda_{\lambda}}\mu^{\prime}
).
The sets
M_{(\lambda,\mu)}
are now tuples
(D,D_{\mu})

with
D\in M_{\lambda}
and
D_{\mu}\in M_{\mu}
, while the basis
elements are
c_{(D,D_{\mu}),(U,U_{\nu})}^{(\lambda,\mu)}
, defined
as in (
2-4
), where we also
indicated the antiinvolution. By construction, this
is a cell datum for
\mathrm{A}
in the sense of
[
GL96
]
.

For the converse one can apply (or rather copy)

[
KX99
, Sections 3 and 4]
: if one
inflates along a non-cellular algebra, then the result can not
be cellular.
∎

2B.
Cell modules

The theory of cellular algebras is particularly nice
for finite-dimensional algebras. This is however not always the
case in the situation we have in mind,
see e.g.
Section 4
. Nevertheless,
parts of the theory still goes through for
infinite-dimensional cellular algebras, see
[
GL96
]
,
[
KX12
]
or
[
ET21
]
. In particular, the
existence of cell modules, cells
and some of their properties, as we will discuss now.

Recall from
Section 2A
that, in pictures, left actions and left multiplications are stacking from the bottom.
For each
\lambda\in\Lambda
and
U\in N_{\lambda}
we have a
left
cell

\mathcal{L}(\lambda,U)
given by

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\lambda,U)=\mathbbm{K}\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid D\in M_{\lambda},b\in\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}\},\quad x\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}=\eqref{eq:cell-mult},

which we endow with the left
\mathrm{A}
-module
structure given above.
(In this paper actions are distinguished from multiplications
by using the symbols
\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}
respectively

\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}
.) In pictures, this means acting on the bottom.
There is also a
right
cell

\mathcal{R}(\lambda,D)

defined verbatim, where the action is from the top.

Lemma 2.2

We have the following.

(a)

The left and right cells are
\mathrm{A}
-modules.

(b)

As
\mathrm{A}
-modules,
\mathcal{L}(\lambda,U)\cong\mathcal{L}(\lambda,U^{\prime})
and

\mathcal{R}(\lambda,D)\cong\mathcal{R}(\lambda,D^{\prime})
for all
U
,
U^{\prime}
and
D
,
D^{\prime}
.

Proof.

This is immediate from the definitions.
∎

Using
Lemma 2.2
,
we will write
\Delta(\lambda)
and
(\lambda)\Delta
(see
also (b) of
Section 2A
) for
any choice of
D\in M_{\lambda},U\in N_{\lambda}
(for the basis elements
of these modules we omit the fixed index).
In the theory of cellular algebras,
these are then also called left, respectively right,
cell modules, so we call them
sandwich cell modules
.

The space
\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}=\mathcal{R}(\lambda,D)\otimes_{\mathrm{A}}\mathcal{L}(\lambda,U)

is called an

\mathcal{H}
-cell
.
Moreover, the space
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}=\mathcal{L}(\lambda,U)\otimes_{\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}}\mathcal{R}(\lambda,D)

is called a two-sided cell or
\mathcal{J}
-cell
.
As free
\mathbbm{K}
-modules we clearly have (cf. part (b) of
Section 2A
)

2C.
Classification of simple modules

For an
\mathrm{A}
-module
M
let

\mathrm{Ann}_{\mathrm{A}}(M)=\{a\in A\mid a\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}M=0\}
be the annihilator.

Definition 2.5

An
apex
of an
\mathrm{A}
-module
M

is a
\lambda\in\Lambda
such that

\mathrm{Ann}_{\mathrm{A}}(M)=\mathcal{J}_{{>_{\Lambda}}\lambda}=\bigcup_{\mu>_{\Lambda}\lambda}\mathcal{J}_{\mu}

and
\phi^{\lambda}
is not constant zero.

Recall that
in the setting of non-unital algebras
simple modules are defined using the usual assumption of
having no non-trivial submodules but one also additionally
assumes that at least one element acts not as zero.

Lemma 2.6

We have the following.

(a)

Every simple
\mathrm{A}
-module
L
has a unique apex

\lambda\in\Lambda
.

(b)

If
\mathbbm{K}
is a field, then the simple modules
L(\lambda,K)

from

have apex
\lambda
.

(c)

A simple
\mathrm{A}
-module
L
of apex
\lambda
is a
simple
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-module. Conversely,
every simple
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-module
L
is a simple

\mathrm{A}
-module
L
with apex
\lambda
, by inflation.

Proof.

One can reformulate e.g.
[
KX12
, Corollary 3.2]

to get the claimed results. (Here we use that
\mathbbm{K}
is
Noetherian and a domain.) Precisely:

(a).
Since
\mathrm{A}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}L\neq 0
there
is a
\leq_{\Lambda}
-minimal
\lambda
such that

\mathcal{J}_{{\geq_{\Lambda}}\lambda}=\bigcup_{\mu\geq_{\Lambda}\lambda}\mathcal{J}_{\mu}
is not contained
in
\mathrm{Ann}_{\mathrm{A}}(M)
.
It is not hard to see
that
\mathrm{Ann}_{\mathrm{A}}(M)
is a maximal
left ideal of
\mathcal{J}_{{\geq_{\Lambda}}\lambda}=\bigcup_{\mu\geq_{\Lambda}\lambda}\mathcal{J}_{\mu}
, so it has to
be
\mathcal{J}_{{>_{\Lambda}}\lambda}
. In particular,

\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}L\neq 0
and actually

\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}L=L
. This can only happen
if some linear combination of the
c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}
is an idempotent.

(b).
By construction.

(c).
By (a), all elements bigger than
\lambda

annihilate
L
which together with the partial ordering
implies that
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}L
, by the same formulas,
and this action is not zero. Since
\mathrm{Ann}_{\mathrm{A}}(L)

is maximal, it follows that

L\cong\mathcal{J}_{{\geq_{\Lambda}}\lambda}/\mathrm{Ann}_{\mathrm{A}}(L)

stays simple as a
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-module.
Conversely, take a simple
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-module
L

and inflate it to a
\mathcal{J}_{{\geq_{\Lambda}}\lambda}
-module
such that its annihilator is
\mathcal{J}_{{>_{\Lambda}}\lambda}
.
Note that
\mathcal{J}_{{\geq_{\Lambda}}\lambda}
is an ideal in

\mathrm{A}
, so
\mathrm{A}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{7.3194pt}{\rotatebox{-90.0}{$\circlearrowright$}}\;\,}L
.
Then the same arguments as in
[
KX12
, Lemma 3.1]

imply that
L
stays simple.
∎

We get an analog of the Clifford–Munn–Ponizovskiĭ theorem (cf.

Section 2A
):

Theorem 2.7

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.

(a)

A
\lambda\in\Lambda
is an apex if and
only if the form
\phi^{\lambda}
is not constant zero
if and only if the form
\phi^{\lambda}_{K}
is not constant zero
for any simple
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
-module
K
. If the assumptions of
hold, then
\lambda\in\Lambda
is an apex if and
only if
r(U,D)\neq 0
for some
D\in M_{\lambda},U\in N_{\lambda}
.

(b)

Assume that
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
is unital and Artinian.
For a fixed apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

the simple
\mathrm{A}
-modules of that apex are
parameterized by simple
modules of
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
. In other words, we have

\displaystyle\left\{\text{simple $\mathrm{A}$-modules with apex $\lambda$}\right\}\xleftrightarrow{1:1}\left\{\text{simple $\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}$-modules}\right\}.

Under this bijection the
simple
\mathrm{A}
-module
L(\lambda,K)

associated to the simple
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}
-module
K

is the head of

\Delta(\lambda,K)
.

(c)

Assume that the assumptions of
hold. For a fixed apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
there exists

\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}
such that there is a 1:1-correspondence

\displaystyle\left\{\text{simple $\mathrm{A}$-modules with apex $\lambda$}\right\}\xleftrightarrow{1:1}\left\{\text{simple $\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}$-modules}\right\}.

Under this bijection the
simple
\mathrm{A}
-module
L(\lambda,K)

for the simple
\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}
-module
K

is the head of the induced module

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}}^{\mathrm{A}}(K)
.

Note that (c) is not a special case of (b) as the sandwiched algebras in (c) need not to be unital and Artinian. This is only relevant in the infinite-dimensional world.

Proof.

(a).
Clearly,
\phi^{\lambda}
is not constant zero
if and only if
\phi^{\lambda}_{K}
is not constant zero. Moreover,

\phi^{\lambda}
being not constant zero implies that

L(\lambda,K)
exists, see
,
and has apex
\lambda
by
Lemma 2.6
. The converse
follows by the definition of an apex.

(c).
First, we choose
\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}
such that
it contains an idempotent
e=1/r(U,D)\cdot c_{D,1,U}^{\lambda}
,
which we can do by (a) and the calculation

1/r(U,D)\cdot c_{D,1,U}^{\lambda}1/r(U,D)\cdot c_{D,1,U}^{\lambda}=1/r(U,D)\cdot c_{D,1,U}^{\lambda}
.
By part (c) of
Lemma 2.6

we can reduce the question to matching simple
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-modules
and simple
\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}
-modules. The picture

shows that
\mathcal{H}_{\lambda,D,U}\cong e\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}e

(note that at least
r(U,D)

is invertible, so
e\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}e\neq 0
).
By a classical theorem of Green, see e.g.

[
GMS09
, Lemma 6]
,
it remains to show that simple
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-modules
are not annihilated by
e
. To see this we observe that
any two pseudo-idempotents of the form
c_{D,1,U}^{\lambda}

are related by appropriate conjugation. That is,
for
e=1/r(U,D)\cdot c_{D,1,U}^{\lambda}
and

e^{\prime}=1/r(U^{\prime},D^{\prime})\cdot c_{D^{\prime},1,U^{\prime}}^{\lambda}
we have

\displaystyle r(U,D)r(U^{\prime},D^{\prime})\cdot e^{\prime}=c_{D^{\prime},1,U}^{\lambda}ec_{D,1,U^{\prime}}^{\lambda},

and all appearing scalars are non-zero, and thus invertible. Hence,
e

annihilates a simple
\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-module
if and only if
e^{\prime}
does. All other
\mathcal{H}
-cells
do not contain idempotents, so a simple

\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
-module can not be annihilated by any
e
in

\mathcal{J}_{\lambda}
.

(b).
The proof is not much different from the one in (c), and follows by well-established arguments in the theory of cellular algebras, see e.g.
[
GL96
]
,
[
KX12
]
,
[
AST18
]
,
[
ET21
]
or
[
GW15
]
. However, the general proof requires
the sandwiched algebras to be unital and Artinian.
∎

Remark 2.7

Note a crucial difference to the case
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}
,
which is (up to having an involution) the cellular case:
one apex can have any number of simples associated to it.

The Brauer algebra as an example

We have also illustrated the antiinvolution
({}_{-})^{\star}
on

\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})
given by vertical mirroring.
Note that Brauer diagrams also make sense in a categorical setting, meaning
with a different number of bottom and top points.

It is known that the Brauer algebra is cellular, see

[
GL96
, Section 4]
or
[
AST18
, Section 5]
.
To make
\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})
cellular one needs

\mathcal{H}
-cells of size one, which is achieved in

[
GL96
, Section 4]
by using
that
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{n}
is
a subalgebra of
\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})
. Then
they work with
the Kazhdan–Lusztig
basis of
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{n}
.
As we will describe now this is not necessary if one wants
to parameterize simple modules.

We let
\Lambda=(\{n,n-2,n-4,\text{...}\},\leq_{\mathbb{N}})\subset\mathbb{N}

with the usual partial order
\leq_{\mathbb{N}}
.
The
\lambda\in\Lambda
are the
through strands
of the Brauer diagrams,
that is, we let the set
M_{\lambda}
consists of all Brauer diagrams
from
n
bottom points to
\lambda
top points. These are the diagrams of the form
D,U
below.
Moreover, we let
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{\lambda}
with the group element basis
\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}
.
As our
\mathbbm{K}
-basis we choose

\displaystyle\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,D,U\in M_{\lambda},b\in\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}\}.

The picture for
n=4
and
\lambda=2
is:

That is, we divide a Brauer diagram into
a diagram only containing caps and crossings, a diagram
only containing cups and crossings, and a part only containing
crossings.

Proposition 2.8

The above defines an involutive sandwich cell datum for
\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})
.

Proof.

Identifying Brauer diagrams with immersed one-dimensional cobordisms
(which is a well-known identification), all axioms are easily verified.
∎

Each
\mathcal{H}
-cell is of size two, and
the colored box is an
\mathcal{H}
-cell
isomorphic to
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{2}
regardless
of
\mathtt{c}
. This is illustrated on the right.

We obtain the well-known classification of simple

\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})
-modules, cf.
[
GL96
, Theorem 4.17]
:

Theorem 2.9

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.

(a)

If
\mathtt{c}\neq 0
, or
\mathtt{c}=0
and
\lambda\neq 0
is odd,
then all
\lambda\in\Lambda
are apexes. In the remaining case,

\mathtt{c}=0
and
\lambda=0
(this only happens if
n
is even),
all
\lambda\in\Lambda-\{0\}
are apexes, but
\lambda=0
is not an apex.

(b)

The simple
\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

are parameterized by simple
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{\lambda}
-modules.

(c)

The simple
\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
can be constructed as
the simple heads of

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{\lambda}}^{\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathtt{c})}(K)
,
where
K
runs over (equivalence classes of)
simple
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{\lambda}
-modules.

Proof.

We apply
Theorem 2.7
.(c) together with the
following observations.

Firstly, we are clearly in the situation of

for the Brauer algebras.
Second, it is easy to see that the
\mathcal{H}
-cells are of a
similar form
as in
Section 2D
, and,
if
\mathtt{c}\neq 0
, then all
\mathcal{H}
-cells are
isomorphic to
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{S}_{\lambda}
.
For
\mathtt{c}=0
and
\lambda\neq 0
, and any
two half-diagrams
we can find an element such that their pairing is one, by
straightening cups-caps.

∎

Remark 2.9

The same strategy works, mutatis mutandis, for the
oriented (or walled) Brauer algebra, other diagram algebras
in the same spirit, e.g. partition algebras, and
the quantum versions of these diagram algebras such as
the Birman–Murakami–Wenzl
algebra (we will treat this case for higher genus in

Section 5
below).
We leave the details to the interested reader.

3.
Handlebody braid and Coxeter groups

Throughout, we fix the
genus

g\in\mathbb{N}
as well as the

number of strands

n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}
. As
a general conventions, all notions involving
g
are vacuous if
g=0
,
and similarly all notions involving
n
are vacuous for
n=1
.

(in

g

Here the numbers indicate the corresponding positions, reading left to right.
We have
usual strands
, illustrated in black, and
core strands
,
illustrated thick and blue-grayish. We note that all of our diagrams have
g
core strands
and
n
usual strands, but we tend to illustrate local pictures,
as we already did above. The elements of the form
\tau_{u}

and their inverses are called
positive coils

and
negative coils
, respectively. We also
say
coils
for short.

Definition 3.0

We let the
handlebody braid group
(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
be the group generated by

\{\tau_{u},\beta_{i}\mid 1\leq u\leq g,1\leq i\leq n-1\}
modulo

(3-2)

\displaystyle\beta_{i}\beta_{j}=\beta_{j}\beta_{i}\;\text{if }|i-j|>1,\quad\beta_{i}\beta_{j}\beta_{i}=\beta_{j}\beta_{i}\beta_{j}\;\text{if }|i-j|=1,

(3-3)

\displaystyle\tau_{u}\beta_{i}=\beta_{i}\tau_{u}\;\text{if }i>1,\quad\tau_{v}(\beta_{1}\tau_{u}\beta_{1})=(\beta_{1}\tau_{u}\beta_{1})\tau_{v}\;\text{if }u\leq v.

We think of
\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
as a
handlebody generalization of the extended affine braid group of type A.
Note that is
\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
not attached to a Coxeter group in any
straightforward way, see e.g.
[
La00
, Remark 4]

and
[
RT21
, (1-7)]
.

Remark 3.0

Special cases of
Section 3A
are:

(a)

The case
g=0
is the classical braid group
\mathrm{B}_{n}=\mathrm{B}_{0,n}
.

(b)

For
g=1
the handlebody braid group is the
braid group of extended affine type A, which
is also the braid group of Coxeter type C
=
B,
see
[
Br73
]
or
[
Al02
]
.

(c)

A perhaps surprising fact is that the handlebody braid group
for
g=2
is
isomorphic to the braid group of affine Coxeter type C,
see
[
Al02
]
.

(d)

To the best of our knowledge the case
g>2
was first
studied in
[
Ve98
]
,
and then further in
[
HOL02
]
.

Remark 3.0

The handlebody braid group describes
the configuration space of a disk with
g
punctures
[
Ve98
]
,

[
La00
]
,

[
HOL02
]
.
Moreover, after taking an appropriate
version of an Alexander closure, as explained e.g. in

[
HOL02
, Theorem 2]
or

[
RT21
, Section 2]

and illustrated in (
3.0
), these braid
groups give an algebraic way to study links in handlebodies.

Proposition 3.1

The handlebody braid group admits the following alternative presentation.

\displaystyle\mathrm{B}_{g,n}\cong\Bigg\langle\begin{gathered}\tilde{\tau}_{u},\,u=1,\text{...},g,\\
\beta_{i},\,i=1,\text{...},n-1\end{gathered}\,\Bigg|\,\scalebox{0.85}{$\begin{gathered}\beta_{i}\beta_{j}=\beta_{j}\beta_{i}\;\text{if }|i-j|>1,\quad\beta_{i}\beta_{j}\beta_{i}=\beta_{j}\beta_{i}\beta_{j}\;\text{if }|i-j|=1,\\
\tilde{\tau}_{u}\beta_{i}=\beta_{i}\tilde{\tau}_{u}\;\text{if }i>1,\quad\tilde{\tau}_{u}\beta_{1}\tilde{\tau}_{u}\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}\tilde{\tau}_{u}\beta_{1}\tilde{\tau}_{u},\quad\\
\tilde{\tau}_{v}(\beta_{1}\tilde{\tau}_{u}\beta_{1}^{-1})=(\beta_{1}\tilde{\tau}_{u}\beta_{1}^{-1})\tilde{\tau}_{v}\;\text{if }u<v\end{gathered}$}\Bigg\rangle.

Proof.

A pleasant exercise (see also e.g.
[
HOL02
, Section 5]
).
∎

arguments and is used several times.

defines an injective group homomorphism

\iota_{g,n}\colon\mathrm{B}_{g,n}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{B}_{g+n}
.

Proof.

Using
Proposition 3.1
, this is

[
Ve98
, Theorem 1]

and
[
La00
, Section 5]
.
∎

We use the presentation without the tildes in this paper, but
the other presentation can also be chosen, if preferred.

3B.
Handlebody Coxeter groups

The appropriate Coxeter groups in this setup are the following.

Definition 3.2

We let the
handlebody Coxeter group
(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
be the quotient group of

\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
by the relations

\displaystyle\beta_{i}^{2}=1\;\text{for }i=1,\text{...},n-1.

We write
t_{u}
and
s_{i}
for the images of

\tau_{u}
respectively
\beta_{i}
in the quotient.

Similarly as for the handlebody braid group
\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
, we think of
Section 3B
as a
handlebody generalization of the extended affine Coxeter group of type A.

The asymmetry in (
3-3
)
vanishes and we have the defining relations:

(3-6)

\displaystyle s_{i}^{2}=1,\quad s_{i}s_{j}=s_{j}s_{i}\;\text{if }|i-j|>1,\quad s_{i}s_{j}s_{i}=s_{j}s_{i}s_{j}\;\text{if }|i-j|=1,

(3-7)

\displaystyle t_{u}s_{i}=s_{i}t_{u}\;\text{if }i>1,\quad t_{v}(s_{1}t_{u}s_{1})=(s_{1}t_{u}s_{1})t_{v}\;\forall u,v.

By (
3-6
)
we see that
we have an embedding of groups
\mathrm{S}_{n}\cong\mathrm{W}_{0,n}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{W}_{g,n}

by identifying the simple transpositions with the
s_{i}
.
Moreover, the
t_{u}
span a free group
\mathrm{F}_{g}\cong\mathrm{W}_{g,1}
,
and
\mathrm{F}_{g}
is thus also a subgroup of
\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
.
We use both below.
Note also that
\mathrm{F}_{g}
, and thus
\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
,
is of infinite order unless
g=0
.
Hence, the analog of
Proposition 3.2

does not hold for
\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
.

Remark 3.2

Special cases of
Section 3B
are:

(a)

The case
g=0
is the symmetric group
\mathrm{S}_{n}
.

(b)

For
g=1
the handlebody Coxeter group is not the
Coxeter group of type C
=
B, but rather the extended affine
Coxeter (Weyl) group of type A.

For the further study of
\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
we use

\mathbb{Z}_{\mathtt{z},Y}=\mathbb{Z}[\mathtt{z}^{\pm 1},Y_{1},\text{...},Y_{g}]
as our ground ring.

Definition 3.2

We define a (right) action
\mathbb{Z}_{\mathtt{z},Y}[X_{1},\text{...},X_{n}]\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}\mathrm{W}_{g,n}

by:

(a)

The generators
s_{i}
act by the permutation action of

\mathrm{S}_{n}
.

(b)

The generators
t_{u}
act by

(3-8)

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} X_{i}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{u}&=\begin{cases}\mathtt{z}^{u}X_{1}+Y_{u}&\text{if }i=1,\\
X_{i}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\\
X_{i}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{u}^{-1}&=\begin{cases}\mathtt{z}^{-u}X_{1}-\mathtt{z}^{-u}Y_{u}&\text{if }i=1,\\
X_{i}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\end{aligned}

The pictorial version of the action (
3-8
) is

Remark 3.2

Special cases of
Section 3B
are:

(a)

The case
g=0
and
\mathtt{z}=1
is the permutation
representation of
\mathrm{S}_{n}
on the polynomial ring

\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\text{...},X_{n}]
.

(b)

The case
g=1
and
\mathtt{z}=1
recovers the usual
polynomial representation of the extended affine Weyl group of type A.

(c)

The case
g=1
,
\mathtt{z}=-1
and
Y_{1}=0
recovers
the root-theoretic version of Tits’ reflection representation
of type C
=
B, i.e. the representation where the type

A
subdiagram acts by permutation and the
additional generator acts as

-1
on
X_{1}
.

Lemma 3.3

The action in
Section 3B
is well-defined.

Proof.

Note that

t_{u}
and
t_{u}^{-1}
act slightly asymmetrically,
but this ensures that their actions invert each other since e.g.

\displaystyle X_{1}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{u}t_{u}^{-1}=(\mathtt{z}^{u}X_{1}+Y_{u})\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{u}^{-1}=\mathtt{z}^{u}t_{u}^{-1}(X_{1})+Y_{u}=\mathtt{z}^{u}(\mathtt{z}^{-u}X_{1}-\mathtt{z}^{-u}Y_{u})+Y_{u}=X_{1}.

Moreover, by construction of the action, the only
non-trivial check is that
(
3-7
) holds.
The left equality in (
3-7
)
is immediate, and for the right we compute

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} X_{1}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{u}s_{1}t_{v}s_{1}=\mathtt{z}^{u}X_{2}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{v}s_{1}+Y_{u}=\mathtt{z}^{u}X_{2}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}s_{1}+Y_{u}&=\mathtt{z}^{u}X_{1}+Y_{u},\\
X_{1}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}s_{1}t_{v}s_{1}t_{u}=X_{2}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{v}s_{1}t_{u}=X_{2}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}s_{1}t_{u}=X_{1}\mathop{\,\;\raisebox{0.0pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{$\circlearrowleft$}}\;\,}t_{u}&=\mathtt{z}^{u}X_{1}+Y_{u}.\end{aligned}

Thus, on the value
X_{1}
the actions agree. Furthermore,
a very similar calculation
shows that they also agree on the value
X_{2}
.
For all other values the relation (
3-7
)
holds evidently.
∎

The action in
Section 3B
is actually
faithful, and this is what we are going to show next.

as follows.
We let

For
i>1
we define

Lemma 3.4

We have

\displaystyle\begin{gathered}L_{u,i}^{\pm 1}L_{u,i}^{\mp 1}=1,\quad\beta_{j}L_{u,i}^{\pm 1}=L_{u,i}^{\pm 1}\beta_{j}\;\text{if }i-1,i\neq j,\\
\beta_{i-1}^{-1}L_{u,i}=L_{u,i-1}\beta_{i-1},\quad\beta_{i}L_{u,i}=L_{u,i+1}\beta_{i}^{-1},\\
\beta_{i-1}L_{u,i}^{-1}=L_{u,i-1}^{-1}\beta_{i-1}^{-1},\quad\beta_{i}^{-1}L_{u,i}^{-1}=L_{u,i+1}^{-1}\beta_{i},\\
L_{u,i}L_{v,j}^{\pm 1}=L_{v,j}^{\pm 1}L_{u,i}\text{ and }L_{u,i}^{-1}L_{v,j}^{\pm 1}=L_{v,j}^{\pm 1}L_{u,i}^{-1}\;\text{if }[v,j]\subset[u,i[,\end{gathered}

where
[v,j]\subset[u,i[
means
u\leq v
and
j<i
.

Proof.

Using topological arguments, all of these are easy
to verify. For example, the middle relations in
(
3.4
) are of the form

Lemma 3.5

Any word in the Jucys–Murphy elements can be ordered
such that
L_{u,i}^{\pm}
appears right=above of

L_{v,j}^{\pm}
only if
j<i
.

Proof.

We use the final relation in (
3.4
)
inductively: First, start with
i=n
and pull
all
L_{u,n}^{\pm}
, for all
u
, to the right=top,
without changing their order (they form a free group).
We freeze these elements in their positions and
we can thus use induction
on the remaining Jucys–Murphy elements
as their maximal second index is
n-1
.
∎

Let us denote the images of the Jucys–Murphy elements
in
\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
by
l_{u,i}^{\pm 1}
.

Lemma 3.6

The set

\displaystyle\left\{l_{u_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}l_{u_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}w\,\middle|\,\begin{gathered}w\in\mathrm{S}_{n},m\in\mathbb{N},\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\\
(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{i})\in(\{1,\text{...},g\}\times\{1,\text{...},n\})^{m},i_{1}\leq\text{...}\leq i_{m}\end{gathered}\right\}

spans
\mathbb{Z}\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
.

Proof.

Since
\tau_{u}=L_{u,1}
, words in

L_{u,i}
and
\beta_{i}
can clearly
generate arbitrary words in
\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
, and thus in

\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
.
Further, using the relations (
3.4
),
we see that we can always pull all

s_{i}\in\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
to the right=top, since

s_{i}=s_{i}^{-1}
. Finally, with the last
relation in (
3.4
) we can order the
L_{u,i}

as claimed, cf.
Lemma 3.5
, which of course
also works for the handlebody Coxeter group.
∎

Proposition 3.7

The set in (
3.6
)
is a
\mathbb{Z}
-basis of
\mathbb{Z}\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
.

Proof.

By
Lemma 3.6
, it only remains to verify that
the elements of the set (
3.6
)
are linearly independent. To this end, we
first observe that we can let
w
be trivial
since the action of
\mathrm{S}_{n}

used in
Lemma 3.6
is
the faithful permutation action. Now, the
only non-trivial action of
l_{u,i}
is on
X_{i}
:

Taking all this together shows that the elements of
(
3.6
) are linearly independent.
∎

Theorem 3.8

The action of
\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
in
Section 3B
is faithful.

Proof.

Directly from the proof of
Proposition 3.7
.
∎

4.
Handlebody Temperley–Lieb and blob algebras

Recall that
\mathbbm{K}
denotes a unital, commutative, Noetherian domain.
The example the reader should keep in mind throughout this section is

\mathbbm{K}=\mathbb{Z}[\boldsymbol{c}]
where
\boldsymbol{c}=(\mathtt{c}_{\gamma})_{\gamma}
is a
collection of variables
\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}

which are circle evaluations.
Recall further that we have fixed
g\in\mathbb{N}
and
n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}
.

4A.
Handlebody Temperley–Lieb algebras

In this section we
consider non-topological

crossingless matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
, which
are all pairings
(i,k)
of integers from
\{1,\text{...},2n\}

such that
i<j<k<l
for all
(i,k)
and
(j,l)
together
with a choice of a reduced word in the free group
\mathrm{F}_{g}

for each appearing pair.

In slightly misleading pictures, cf.
Section 4A
,
these are crossingless matchings of
2n
points where usual strands
can wind around the cores, but not among themselves.
Here we use the same conventions as in
Section 3
in the sense
that all cores are to the left.
For example, if
g=3
and
n=2
, then

are examples of such crossingless matchings.

Remark 4.0

We will use a similar notation as in

Section 3
, e.g.
\tau_{u}
for elements
as illustrated on the right in (
4-1
).

These crossingless matchings are not allowed to have
any circles (circles, by definition, are a connected components of usual strings not touching the bottom or top).
But such circles, as usual for these types of algebras, could appear after concatenation. To address this we need to associate circles in such diagrams to conjugacy classes in
\mathrm{F}_{g}
.

To this end, for each circle in the diagrams we will
associate a word in
\mathrm{F}_{g}
by starting somewhere
generic on the circle, say the rightmost point, and read clockwise.
This gives an element of
\mathrm{F}_{g}
, keeping the identification of
coils and generators of
\mathrm{F}_{g}
in mind, associated to each circle
which is well-defined up to conjugacy. We then say the circles are
\mathrm{F}_{g}
-colored
, meaning
tuples of a circle and a representative of a conjugacy class in
\mathrm{F}_{g}
. These circles will index our parameters momentarily.

For the
following definition we choose a set of parameters

\boldsymbol{c}=(\mathtt{c}_{\gamma})_{\gamma}\in\mathbbm{K}
, one for
each
\mathrm{F}_{g}
-colored circle
\gamma
. Thus, the parameters
are constant on conjugacy classes in
\mathrm{F}_{g}
.

Definition 4.0

The evaluation of
a
\mathrm{F}_{g}
-colored circle
\gamma
is defined to be the removal
of a closed component, contributing a factor

\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}
. We call this
circle evaluation
.

We could choose all
\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}
to be different
or equal, there is no restriction on the choice of these parameters
(see however
Section 4A
below).
Note that all non-essential circles are associated to
the trivial coloring
\gamma=1
and are evaluated to
\mathtt{c}_{1}
.

The first word in
\mathrm{F}_{g}
is the trivial word,
the second is
uv
, and the third is
u^{2}v
.

To each usual strand in a crossingless matching we associate
a word in
\mathrm{F}_{g}
by starting at the rightmost boundary point
of the string and read to the other one, again using the
identification of coils and generators of
\mathrm{F}_{g}
.
A
\mathrm{F}_{g}
-colored concatenation
of
crossingless matchings
x
and
y
of
2n
points of genus
g

is, up to colors, a concatenation
xy
in the usual sense
and the colors are concatenated reading bottom to top along
the strings respectively starting anywhere and moving
clockwise along closed components.

Definition 4.0

We let
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
,
the
handlebody Temperley–Lieb algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
), be
the algebra whose underlying free
\mathbbm{K}
-module is the

\mathbbm{K}
-linear span of all
crossingless matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
, and
with multiplication given by
\mathrm{F}_{g}
-colored
concatenation of diagrams modulo
circle evaluation.

Remark 4.0

There are various ways to define
Temperley–Lieb algebras beyond the classical case
and some of them are not topological in nature, and
the construction in
Section 4A

is one of those that are not topological.
In particular,
the
Kauffman skein relation

For completeness we note an easy fact:

Lemma 4.1

The algebra
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
is an associative, unital
algebra with a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis given by all crossingless
matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
.

Proof.

Note that the
\mathrm{F}_{g}
-colored
concatenation of closed components ensures that the
circle evaluation only depends on the associated word in
\mathrm{F}_{g}

modulo conjugation.
Thus, the only claim which is not immediate is
that the
\mathrm{F}_{g}
-colored
concatenation is associative. This however follows
by identifying the colors by dots on the strings.
∎

Note that the algebra
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
is
infinite-dimensional unless
g=0
, since the group-like elements
\tau_{u}

are of infinite order and span
\mathrm{F}_{g}\cong\mathrm{TL}_{g,1}(\boldsymbol{c})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Remark 4.1

For low genus
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
is well-studied
(although for
g>0
the precise definitions and the
nomenclature vary
throughout the literature):

(a)

For
g=0
the algebra

\mathrm{TL}_{0,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
is the
Temperley–Lieb algebra in its crossingless matching definition.

(b)

In case
g=1
there are the so-called
affine Temperley–Lieb algebra or the
type C
=
B Temperley–Lieb algebra
(the name comes from the relation of this algebra
to the braid group of type C
=
B
as recalled in
Section 3A
),
which were studied in many works such as e.g.
[
GL98
]
.
The algebra
\mathrm{TL}_{1,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
is a version of these.

(c)

Similarly, for

g=2
there is a so-called two-boundary
Temperley–Lieb algebra
and an affine type C Temperley–Lieb
algebra, again independently
introduced in many works.
The algebra
\mathrm{TL}_{2,n}(\boldsymbol{c})

is a version of these.

Note that Temperley–Lieb algebras for
g<2

are sometimes assumed to satisfy a quadratic relation for the coil
elements, but we do not assume that.
These algebras are studied in
the sections below.

Similarly as in
Section 2D
,
we let
\Lambda=\big(\{n,n-2,n-4,\text{...}\},\leq_{\mathbb{N}}\big)\subset\mathbb{N}

with the usual partial order.
The
\lambda\in\Lambda
are again the through strands of our diagrams,
and we let
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{F}_{g}
,
the group ring of the free group in
g

generators
\mathrm{F}_{g}\cong\mathrm{Br}_{g,1}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Br}_{g,\lambda}
. We take the group element basis of
\mathrm{F}_{g}
as the sandwich basis
\mathrm{B}_{\lambda}
.

Remark 4.1

We assume that
\mathrm{Br}_{g,\lambda}

is trivial if
\lambda=0
.
In particular,
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{F}_{g}\cong\mathbbm{K}
for
\lambda=0
, since
we identify
\mathrm{F}_{g}
with a subgroup of
\mathrm{Br}_{g,\lambda}
,
and the latter is trivial for
\lambda=0
.

The construction of the basis

(4-4)

\displaystyle\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,D,U\in M_{\lambda},b\in\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}\}

works mutatis mutandis as for the
classical Temperley–Lieb algebra, having a concatenation
of a cup diagram
D
, a cup diagram
U
and through strands
b
, but now
the caps and cups are allowed to wind around the cores
(but not the through strands),
and we have coils of through strands in the middle.
The following picture clarifies the construction:

\mathrm{F}_{g}

Proposition 4.2

The above defines an
involutive sandwich cell datum for
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Proof.

It is clear that one can cut any crossingless matching
of
2n
points of genus
g
uniquely into pieces as
illustrated in (
4-5
), hence that
(
4-4
) is a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis follows.
So it remains to verify (
2-1
).
That the multiplication is ordered with respect to through
strands follows (as for the classical Temperley–Lieb algebra)
from the fact that one can not remove cups and caps, they
can only be created. All the other requirements are clear by
construction; one basically calculates

Theorem 4.3

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.

(a)

If
\boldsymbol{c}\neq 0
, or
\boldsymbol{c}=0
and
\lambda\neq 0
is odd,
then all
\lambda\in\Lambda
are apexes. In the remaining case,

\boldsymbol{c}=0
and
\lambda=0
(this only happens if
n
is even),
all
\lambda\in\Lambda-\{0\}
are apexes, but
\lambda=0
is not an apex.

(b)

The simple
\mathrm{TL}_{n,g}(\boldsymbol{c})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

are parameterized by simple modules of
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{F}_{g}
.

(c)

The simple
\mathrm{TL}_{n,g}(\boldsymbol{c})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
can be constructed as
the simple heads of

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{F}_{g}}^{\mathrm{TL}_{n,g}(\boldsymbol{c})}(K)
,
where
K
runs over (equivalence classes of)
simple
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{F}_{g}
-modules.

Proof.

Word-by-word as for the Brauer algebra,
see the proof of
Theorem 2.9
. In particular,
this is a direct application of
Theorem 2.7
.
∎

.

coming from

, and move
freely along strands in a vertical direction, but can not pass one another:

Indeed, in a topological model that is possible. However, as we will
explore more carefully in
Section 4D
,
these diagrams will not be topological in nature, but
have some error terms. So we decided to
keep blobs to the left from the start.

Using the same reading conventions as for
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
but
counting types of blobs instead of coils, we can associated a word in
\mathrm{F}_{g}

to usual strands and circles. As before, all parameters
below will be assumed to be constant on conjugacy classes.

Fix
cyclotomic parameters

\boldsymbol{b}=(\mathtt{b}_{u,i})\in\mathbbm{K}^{d_{1}+\text{...}+d_{g}}
.
We also fix
\boldsymbol{d}=(\mathtt{d}_{u})\in\mathbb{N}^{g}
called the
degree vector
.
Note that concatenation can create circles with blobs.
For each such circle
\gamma
with
at most
\mathtt{d}_{u}-1
blobs of the corresponding kind
we choose a parameter
\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}\in\mathbbm{K}
, whose collection
is denoted by
\boldsymbol{c}=(\mathtt{c}_{\gamma})_{\gamma}
.

Definition 4.3

The evaluation of
a closed circle
\gamma
is defined to be the removal
of a closed component, contributing a factor

\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}
. We call this
blob circle evaluation
.

Example 4.3

The circle evaluation of the handlebody Temperley–Lieb
algebra becomes
blob circle evaluation, e.g.

Note that circles with more than
\mathtt{d}_{u}-1

blobs of the corresponding kind
can be evaluated by using (
4-8
) and the
above circle evaluation, so we do not need to define their evaluation.

Definition 4.3

We let the (cyclotomic)
handlebody blob algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
be
the algebra whose underlying
\mathbbm{K}
-vector space is the

\mathbbm{K}
-linear span of all
blob diagrams on
2n
points of genus
g
,
with multiplication given by concatenation of diagrams modulo
blob circle evaluation, and the two-sided ideal
generated by the
cyclotomic relations

(4-8)

\displaystyle(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,1})\varpi_{1}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,2})\varpi_{2}\text{...}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,\mathtt{d}_{u}-1})\varpi_{d_{u}-1}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,\mathtt{d}_{u}})=0,

where
\varpi_{j}
is any finite (potentially empty)
word in
b_{v}
for
v\neq u
.

In words, any occurrence of
\mathtt{d}_{u}
blobs colored
g

on a strand can be replaced by the corresponding expression
in the expansion of (
4-8
).

\mathtt{d}_{1}=1

\mathtt{d}_{2}=2

Note that the final expression can be resolved in two ways: First
by removing the blob colored 1, and then by replacing the two blobs colored 2
by one blob colored 2. Second, by applying (
4-8
)
directly, as we did above.
Both give the same result.

Remark 4.3

We have not defined

\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})

as a quotient of
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})

because blobs would be invertible
if we define them as the image of
\tau_{u}
in the quotient
and we want to include the possibility of blobs being nilpotent,
cf.
Section 4B
.

Note that however that for certain choices of parameters
the blobs are invertible, and
\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})

is often a quotient of
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
for these parameters.

Remark 4.3

We again discuss a few instances of
Section 4B
:

(a)

For
g=0
the blob and the Temperley–Lieb algebra
coincide.

(b)

The algebra
\mathrm{Bl}_{1,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})

is sometimes called the (cyclotomic) blob algebra, see e.g.
[
MS94
]
.

(c)

In genus
g=2
there is a two-boundary
blob algebra, see e.g.

[
dGN09
]
(beware that the version of
\mathrm{Bl}_{2,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})

in that paper is called a two-boundary
Temperley–Lieb algebra).

For
g>0

the terminology in the literature is not consistent, and
Temperley–Lieb algebras and blob algebras might
be the same or not. For us
Section 4B

generalizes
[
MS94
]
.

We need the
analog of
Lemma 4.1
which reads as follows.

Lemma 4.4

The algebra

\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
is an associative, unital
algebra with a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis given by all handlebody blob diagrams
on
2n
points of genus

g
where all strands have at most
\mathtt{d}_{u}

blobs of the corresponding type.

Proof.

The only fact to observe is that
the cyclotomic condition (
4-8
)
ensures that it suffices to
fix an evaluation for any circle whose number of blobs are bounded
by the degree vector.
∎

For our fixed genus
g
and degree vector
\boldsymbol{d}
we define
the (corresponding)
blob numbers
using multinomial
coefficients:

(4-9)

\displaystyle\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq k_{u}\leq\min(k,\mathtt{d}_{u}-1)\\
k_{1}+\text{...}+k_{g}=k\end{subarray}}\binom{k}{k_{1},\text{...},k_{g}},

where the sums run over all
k\in\mathbb{N}
and all

0\leq k_{u}\leq\min(k,\mathtt{d}_{u}-1)
,
for
u\in\{1,\text{...},g\}
, that sum up to
k
.
Note that this sum is finite.

Example 4.4

We have
\mathtt{BN}_{0,\boldsymbol{d}}=1
(by definition),

\mathtt{BN}_{1,\boldsymbol{d}}=\mathtt{d}_{1}
and, for
\mathtt{d}_{1}=2
and
\mathtt{d}_{2}=3
,
we get
\mathtt{BN}_{2,\boldsymbol{d}}=\binom{0}{0,0}+\binom{1}{1,0}+\binom{1}{0,1}+\binom{2}{1,1}+\binom{2}{0,2}+\binom{3}{1,2}=9
.
Note that there are nine blob diagrams
with one strand and at most one
1
blob and two
2
blobs:

In fact, we have

\mathtt{BN}_{2,\boldsymbol{d}=(\mathtt{d}_{1},\mathtt{d}_{2})}=\binom{\mathtt{d}_{1}+\mathtt{d}_{2}}{\mathtt{d}_{1}}-1
.

Lemma 4.5

For any
\boldsymbol{c}
, we have an isomorphism of algebras

\displaystyle\mathrm{Bl}_{g,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})\cong\mathbbm{K}\langle b_{u}\mid u\in\{1,\text{...},g\}\rangle/\eqref{eq:cyclotomic-blob}.

In particular,

\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Bl}_{g,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})=\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}
.

Proof.

Since blobs do not satisfy any other relation than (
4-8
),
the only claim that is not immediate is the dimension count.
To see that that works, we recall that the multinomial coefficient

\binom{k}{a_{1},\text{...},a_{g}}

counts the appearance of
x^{a_{1}}_{1}\text{...}x^{a_{g}}_{g}
in the expansion
of
(x_{1}+\text{...}+x_{g})^{k}
, which is the counting problem we need to solve.
Finally, note that
b_{u}^{d_{u}}
can be expressed in terms of
lower order expressions, which explains our condition on the summation.
∎

We also calculate the dimension of

\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
:

Proposition 4.6

We have
\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Bl}_{g,0}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})=1
,

\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Bl}_{g,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})=\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}
and

(4-10)

\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})=\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}{\textstyle\sum_{k\in\{2,4,6,\text{...},2n\}}}\,C_{k-1}\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n-k}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c}),

where
C_{k-1}
is the
(k-1)
th Catalan number.

The proof of
Proposition 4.6

is an inductive argument which works in quite some
generality and that we learned from
[
tD94
]
.

Proof.

By
Lemma 4.4
, it suffices to count
handlebody blob diagrams of genus
g
.

We then argue by induction on
n
.
The induction start is clear, so let
n>1
.
First, the
strand with the leftmost point can end at position
2k
for
k\in\mathbb{N}
,
and one can divide the diagram into two parts: a part underneath it

TL_{k-1}
and a part to the right of it
BL_{n-k}
. For example,

The part underneath it, denoted
TL_{k-1}
above,
can not carry any blobs, so the number of possible diagrams is the same
as for the corresponding Temperley–Lieb algebra, which is the Catalan
number appearing in (
4-10
). The number of possible diagrams
on the right, denoted
BL_{n-k}
above, is the dimension of

\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n-k}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
,
and we get the corresponding
number in (
4-10
). The remaining number is
the number of possible blob placements on the
strand with the leftmost point, see
Lemma 4.5
.
∎

Example 4.6

For
g=0
one obtains that

\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Bl}_{0,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})=C_{n}
, which is
of course expected. For
g=1
one can solve
the recursion in (
4-10
) and obtains

\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Bl}_{1,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})=\binom{2n}{n}
,
the dimension of the blob algebra, cf.
[
Gr98
, Lemma 5.7]
.

Regarding cellular structures, the same strategy as for
the handlebody Temperley–Lieb algebra from

Section 4A

works. Precisely, the
D
part is allowed to have caps
with blobs and through strands without blobs,
the
U
part is allowed to have cups
with blobs and through strands without blobs, and the middle
has blobs on through strands.
The picture to keep in mind is

Note that the middle part is
\mathbb{S}_{0}=\mathbbm{K}
and

\displaystyle\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}=\mathbbm{K}\langle b_{u}\mid u\in\{1,\text{...},g\}\rangle/\eqref{eq:cyclotomic-blob}.

We choose the monomial basis in the
b_{u}
as our
sandwich basis.
As the antiinvolution we choose the map

({}_{-})^{\star}\colon\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})\to\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
that mirrors
diagrams and fixes all blobs.

Proposition 4.7

The above defines an
involutive sandwich cell datum for
\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Proof.

The proof is, mutatis mutandis, as in
Proposition 4.2
and omitted.
∎

The cells look similar as in
Section 4A
.

Theorem 4.8

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.

(a)

If
\boldsymbol{c}\neq 0
, or
\boldsymbol{c}=0
and
\lambda\neq 0
is odd,
then all
\lambda\in\Lambda
are apexes. In the remaining case,

\boldsymbol{c}=0
and
\lambda=0
(this only happens if
n
is even), all
\lambda\in\Lambda-\{0\}
are apexes, but
\lambda=0
is not an apex.

(b)

The simple
\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

are parameterized by simple modules of
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
.

(c)

The simple
\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
can be constructed as
the simple heads of

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})}(K)
,
where
K
runs over (the equivalence classes of)
simple
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
-modules.

Proof.

This can be proven verbatim as in the previous cases, see e.g.

Theorem 2.9
.
∎

The sandwiched algebras are identified in

Lemma 4.5
. Thus,
Theorem 4.8

explicitly gives the desired
classification of simple
\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
-modules.

Example 4.8

The low genus cases of
Theorem 4.8
are known
(for simplicity we ignore the potential exception
for
\lambda=0
in the text below):

(a)

For
g=0
we have
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{0,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}=\mathbbm{K}
, so we obtains
the classical parametrization of the simple modules of
the Temperley–Lieb algebra by through strands.

(b)

For
g=1
we have that
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{1,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
is
a finite-dimensional quotient of a polynomial ring in one variable
b

by an ideal of the form

\displaystyle(b-\mathtt{b}_{1})\text{...}(b-\mathtt{b}_{\mathtt{d}_{1}})=0.

In particular, the number of simple modules associated to

\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{1,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
equals the number of distinct
parameters in
\boldsymbol{b}
. For example, if
\mathtt{d}_{1}=2
, then

\displaystyle\mathtt{b}_{1}=\mathtt{b}_{2}=0\Rightarrow\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{1,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}\cong\mathbbm{K}[b]/(b^{2})\text{ has one simple module},

\displaystyle\mathtt{b}_{1}=1,\mathtt{b}_{2}=0\Rightarrow\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{1,1}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}\cong\mathbbm{K}[b]/(b-1)b\text{ has two simple modules}.

In the latter case
b^{2}=b
,
which is the situation studied in
[
MS94
]
.
Thus, we recover the classification of simples of the blob
algebra from
[
MS94
]
.

4C.
Topology of handlebody Temperley–Lieb algebras

Another way of defining the classical Temperley–Lieb algebra
would be as the quotient of the algebra of tangles by circle
evaluation and the Kauffman skein relation. To discuss
a handlebody analog let us define
handlebody
(framed) tangle diagrams of
2n

points of genus
g
, using handlebody braid
diagrams as in
Section 3
and inspired
by
Proposition 3.2
, as the (isotopy classes of) tangle
diagrams in
g+n
strings, which are pure on the first
g
strings, modulo
the usual tangle relations.
The framing is given by a vector field pointing to the
g
th core strand
from the left.

As before we fix circle
evaluations
\boldsymbol{c}=(\mathtt{c}_{\gamma})_{\gamma}
, one for any isotopy
class of circles
\gamma
.
We also fix any invertible
element
\mathtt{q}\in\mathbbm{K}
that has a square root in
\mathbbm{K}
.

Definition 4.8

The evaluation of a circle
\gamma
is defined to be the removal
of a closed component, contributing a factor

\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}
. We call this
circle evaluation
.

Definition 4.8

We let the
topological handlebody Temperley–Lieb algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})
be the
algebra whose underlying free
\mathbbm{K}
-module is the

\mathbbm{K}
-linear span of all
handlebody tangle diagrams of
2n
points of genus
g
, and
with multiplication given by concatenation of diagrams modulo
circle evaluation and (
4-2
).

Note that
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
and

\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})
are very different algebras.
For example, as we have seen in (
4-3
),
the coils are of finite order
in
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})
but of infinite
order in
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Remark 4.8

(a)

For
g=0

Section 4C

is a classical definition, while the
case
g=1
is related by Schur–Weyl duality
to Verma modules, see
[
ILZ21
]
.

(b)

Without evaluation of circles the case

g>2
can also be found in

[
ILZ21
]
under the name multi-polar,
but not much appears to be known.

Lemma 4.9

The algebra

\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})
is an associative, unital
algebra with a
\mathbbm{K}
-spanning set given by all crossingless
matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
where each coil is positive and appears at most of order
1
.

Proof.

That the claimed set is spanning is clear by circle evaluation and
(
4-3
).
∎

Recall that
C_{n}
denotes the
n
th Catalan
number, which is also the dimension of the
genus
g=0
Temperley–Lieb algebra.

Definition 4.9

We call parameters
\boldsymbol{c}=(\mathtt{c}_{\gamma})_{\gamma}
such that

\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})\geq C_{n}

weakly admissible
.

With
Section 4A
in mind, the
following is in contrast to
Lemma 4.1

a non-trivial result. To state it let

[k]_{\mathtt{q}}=\mathtt{q}^{k-1}+\text{...}+\mathtt{q}^{-k+1}
denote
the usual quantum number for
k\in\mathbb{N}
, and
note that
for the choice
\boldsymbol{c}=(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}})

the algebra
\mathrm{TL}_{G}(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}})=\mathrm{TL}_{0,G}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})

is the classical Temperley–Lieb algebra on
G
strands
whose circle evaluates to
-[2]_{\mathtt{q}}
.

Lemma 4.10

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.
For any
\mathtt{q}\in\mathbbm{K}
and
G\geq g
such that

[k]_{\mathtt{q}}\neq 0

for all
k<G+1
there exists
a set
\boldsymbol{c}^{G}
and an algebra homomorphisms
(explicitly given in the proof below)

\displaystyle\iota^{G}\colon\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c}^{G})\to\mathrm{TL}_{G+n}\big(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}}\big).

Moreover, the parameters
\boldsymbol{c}^{G}
are weakly admissible.

Note that the assumptions in
Lemma 4.10

are always satisfied for e.g.
\mathbbm{K}=\mathbb{C}(\mathtt{q}^{1/2})

and
\mathtt{q}
being the generic variable.

Proof.

For the algebra
\mathrm{TL}_{G+n}\big(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}}\big)

there exists a Jones–Wenzl idempotent
\mathtt{e}_{G}

on
G
strands, see e.g.

[
KL94
, Chapter 3]

(strictly speaking
[
KL94
, Chapter 3]
uses

\mathbbm{K}=\mathbb{C}(\mathtt{q})
but under the assumption that
[k]\neq 0

for all
k<G+1
the whole discussion therein goes though as long as
the number of strands is less than
G+1
),
and we can consider the idempotent truncation

\mathtt{e}_{G}\mathrm{TL}_{G}\big(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}}\big)\mathtt{e}_{G}
.
By the properties of
\mathtt{e}_{G}
we have

\mathtt{e}_{G}\mathrm{TL}_{G}\big(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}}\big)\mathtt{e}_{G}\cong\mathbbm{K}\{\mathtt{e}_{G}\}
,
so for any circle
\gamma
in
\mathtt{e}_{G}\mathrm{TL}_{G}(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}})\mathtt{e}_{G}

we get a scalar
\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}^{G}
.
Fix some partitioning of
G=M_{1}+\text{...}+M_{g}
for
M_{i}\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}
.
With the choices
\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}^{G}
it is easy to see that
blowing the
i
th core strand into
M_{i}
parallel strands
and flanking them then with
\mathtt{e}_{G}

defines an algebra homomorphism

\displaystyle\iota\colon\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c}^{G})\to(\mathtt{e}_{G}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{n})\mathrm{TL}_{G+n}\big(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}}\big)(\mathtt{e}_{G}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{n})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{TL}_{G+n}\big(-[2]_{\mathtt{q}}\big).

The pictures illustrating the above constructions are

(4-12)

where the boxes represent the Jones–Wenzl idempotent
\mathtt{e}_{G}
.
To see the remaining statement let
\mathrm{Sym}^{G}_{\mathtt{q}}(\mathbbm{K}^{2})

denote the
G
th quantum symmetric power of
\mathbbm{K}^{2}
.
We use
\iota

and quantum symmetric Howe duality

[
RT16
, Theorem 2.6 (1) and (2)]

(which work over
\mathbb{Z}[\mathtt{q},\mathtt{q}^{-1}]
) in combination with

[
RT16
, Proposition 2.14]
(which works
under the assumptions on
[k]_{\mathtt{q}}

to the point needed) to define
a representation of
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c}^{G})

on
\mathrm{Sym}^{G}_{\mathtt{q}}(\mathbbm{K}^{2})\otimes\mathbbm{K}^{2}\otimes\text{...}\otimes\mathbbm{K}^{2}
.
Using this representation one can check that

\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c}^{G})
can not be trivial since,
for example,
\mathrm{TL}_{0,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c}^{G})

acts faithfully by classical Schur–Weyl duality.
∎

Remark 4.10

Our proof of
Lemma 4.10
is directly
inspired by
[
RT21
]
: As pointed out in that paper,
the handlebody closing (
3.0
) can
be interpreted, in the appropriate
algebraic framework, by putting an idempotent on bottom and top.
Moreover and alternatively to the usage of
(growing) symmetric powers, one might want to associate Verma modules
to the core strands as in the
g=1
case, see
[
ILZ21
]
.
This approach has however the disadvantage that we do not know analogs
of Jones–Wenzl idempotents which one could use to get
coherent circle evaluations.

Remark 4.10

For
\mathtt{q}\in\mathbbm{K}
being a root of unity and
\mathbbm{K}
being a field
there are still Jones–Wenzl
type idempotents, see e.g.
[
MS22
]
or
[
STWZ21
]

for general constructions of such idempotents. However their
endomorphism spaces are no longer trivial, so we can not use the
argument in the proof of
Lemma 4.10
.

We do not know any explicit condition to check
whether parameter choices are
admissible
, meaning
that we do not know a
“generic” basis of
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})
.
We leave it to future work to find such a basis.

4D.
Topology of handlebody blob algebras

The purpose of this section is to explain a different
presentation for
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Remark 4.10

We will also use a similar construction as
presented in this section for
cyclotomic handlebody Brauer and BMW algebras later on,
so we decided to spell it out here despite

Lemma 4.11
.
However, while the topological handlebody
blob algebra is the same as the topological handlebody
Temperley–Lieb algebra, this phenomena is no longer true for
handlebody Brauer and BMW algebras.

Definition 4.10

Retain the notation and conventions from
Section 4C
. We let the
topological handlebody blob algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})

be the subalgebra of

\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})

spanned by all elements containing only positive coils.

Lemma 4.11

We have
\mathrm{Bl}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})=\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}^{\mathrm{top}}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Proof.

Clear by (
4-3
).
∎

To give a different diagrammatic presentation
we need the notion of
blobbed presentations
, that will
spell out now.
The construction of this works mutatis mutandis
as in
Section 4B

(so we will be brief)
with one main difference:
we allow crossings between the usual strands.
This gives us the notion of

framed tangled blob diagrams of
2n
points of genus
g
,
where blobs move freely around its strand,
but always keep being reachable from the left, and do not pass
each other, cf. (
4-7
).

Examples of such tangled blob diagrams and how they relate
to the diagrammatic used in

Section 4C
are

The relations in (
4-14
) and (
4-17
)
are called
blob slides
.
Also note the distorted topology in
Lemma 4.12
,
which is however gets resolved for
\mathtt{q}=1
.

Proof.

Relations (
4-14
) are
a blob version of the equalities

\beta_{i-1}^{-1}L_{u,i}=L_{u,i-1}\beta_{i-1}
and

\beta_{i}L_{u,i}=L_{u,i+1}\beta_{i}^{-1}

between Jucys–Murphy elements, cf.
Lemma 3.4
.

To prove the first relation
in (
4-15
) slide down the blob on the
right and use (
4-13
) to
write it as a blob on the strand to the left.
The rest follows from (
4-11
).
The second relation in (
4-15
)
is proved analogously.

Relation (
4-16
)
in the case
v\geq u
is the last
relation in
Lemma 3.4
.
In the case
v\leq u
we calculate

\displaystyle\hbox to35.55pt{\vbox to30.78pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-27.2604pt\lower-0.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}

5.
Handlebody Brauer and BMW algebras

We will be brief in this section as it is very similar
to the previous discussions. Recall that we have fixed the genus
g
and
the number of strands
n
.

5A.
Handlebody Brauer and BMW algebras

We use handlebody
(framed) tangle diagrams of
2n

points of genus
g
as in
Section 4C
.
We fix invertible scalars

\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a}\in\mathbbm{K}
with
\mathtt{q}\neq\mathtt{q}^{-1}
.
Circles that may appear after concatenation of these diagrams
are evaluated as in
Section 4C
, and we
fix
\mathtt{c}_{\gamma}\in\mathbbm{K}
as before, except for

\mathtt{c}_{1}
which we define as

\displaystyle\mathtt{c}_{1}=1+\frac{\mathtt{a}-\mathtt{a}^{-1}}{\mathtt{q}-\mathtt{q}^{-1}}.

Definition 5.0

We let the
handlebody BMW algebra
(in
n
strands and
of genus
g
)
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
be
the algebra whose underlying free
\mathbbm{K}
-module is the

\mathbbm{K}
-linear span of all
handlebody tangle diagrams of
2n
points
of genus
g
, and
with multiplication given by concatenation of diagrams modulo
circle evaluation, and the
skein
relation
(
5-1
) and (
5-2
):

For
\mathtt{q}=\mathtt{q}^{-1}
we also let
\mathtt{a}=\mathtt{a}^{-1}

and let
\mathtt{c}_{1}\in\mathbbm{K}
be any parameter.

Definition 5.0

We call the specialization
\mathtt{q}=\mathtt{a}=1
the
Brauer
specialization
and the resulting algebra
the
handlebody Brauer algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Remark 5.0

Note that
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
is
not a specialization of
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

as the
\mathtt{q}=\mathtt{a}=1
limit of
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

has
\mathtt{c}_{1}=2
. This technicality will not play any role for us, so
we strategically ignore it.

In the specialization
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
we can
use a simplified notation for the crossings

Remark 5.0

Special cases of
Section 5A
have
appeared in the literature:

(a)

The case
g=0
is the case of the
Birman–Murakami–Wenzl algebra, respectively Brauer algebra,
and is classical.

(b)

For
g=1
these algebras appear under the name
of affine BMW or Brauer algebras in many works, e.g. in

[
HO01a
]
or
[
OR04
]
.

(c)

For
g=2
we were not able to find a reference, but the
definition is easily deduced from the affine type C
braid group combinatorics. However, this would give
a two-boundary version of the above, with one
core strand to the left and one to the right,
see e.g.
[
DR18
]
for the
corresponding pictures.

In order to define a spanning set for

\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
we
need the notion of

perfect matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
: these are
perfect matchings of
2n
points where strands can wind around the cores.
We keep the conventions of the
previous sections and consider that all cores are at the left.
For example, if
g=3
and
n=2
, then

are examples of such perfect matchings.
These perfect matchings are equal if they describe the same perfect matching
with the same winding around cores.

Remark 5.0

With blobs the situation is trickier
because we need to be careful
with relation (
4-15
).
Without blobs we do not have this problem and we can treat
these perfect matchings as topological objects.

Forgetting isotopy, each perfect matching as above defines an element of

\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

by lifting crossings.
