Now we can proceed as before:

Lemma 5.1

The algebra

\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\mathtt{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
is an associative, unital
algebra with a
\mathbbm{K}
-spanning set given by positive lifts
of perfect matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
.

Proof.

Clear by (
5-1
) and (
5-2
), and isotopies.
∎

The dimension bound in the next definition
comes from the classical Brauer/BMW algebra.
That is, the number
(2n-1)!!

in the definition of weakly admissible parameters up next
is the dimension of the classical BMW and Brauer algebras.

Definition 5.1

We call parameters
(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
such that the
\mathbbm{K}
-spanning set
in
Lemma 5.1
is a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis

admissible
. We call parameters
weakly admissible

if
\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\mathtt{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})\geq(2n-1)!!
.

To state the analog of
Lemma 4.10
denote by
\mathrm{BMW}_{G+n}(\mathtt{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})=\mathrm{BMW}_{0,G+n}(\mathtt{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

the classical BMW algebra in
G+n
strands.

Lemma 5.2

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.
For any choice of
\mathtt{q}\in\mathbbm{K}
and
G\geq g
such that

[k]_{\mathtt{q}}\neq 0

for all
1\ll k
there exists
a triple
(\boldsymbol{c}^{G},\mathtt{q}^{G},\mathtt{a}^{G})
and
an algebra homomorphisms
(explicitly given in the proof below)

\displaystyle\iota^{G}\colon\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c}^{G},\mathtt{q}^{G},\mathtt{a}^{G})\to\mathrm{BMW}_{G+n}(\tilde{\mathtt{c}},\tilde{\mathtt{q}},\tilde{\mathtt{a}}).

Moreover, the parameters
(\boldsymbol{c}^{G},\mathtt{q}^{G},\mathtt{a}^{G})
are
weakly admissible.

If
\mathtt{q}
is not a root of unity, then there is
always a corresponding triple
(\boldsymbol{c}^{G},\mathtt{q}^{G},\mathtt{a}^{G})
.

Proof.

Denote by
(\tilde{\boldsymbol{c}},\tilde{\mathtt{q}},\tilde{\mathtt{a}})

a choice of parameters such that Schur–Weyl–Brauer duality
(for this duality
we refer the reader to, for example,
[
AST17
, Theorem 3.17]

and
[
Hu11
, Theorem 1.3]
)
gives a well-defined algebra homomorphism from

\mathrm{BMW}_{G+n}(\tilde{\mathtt{c}},\mathtt{q},\tilde{\mathtt{a}})

into the endomorphism space of the (
G+n
)-fold
tensor product of the vector representation of an associated quantum
group of types
BCD
, called tensor space.
The proof is then essentially the same as the one in

Lemma 4.10
, using
Schur–Weyl–Brauer duality instead of
(a special case of) Schur–Weyl duality. Precisely,
we define
\iota^{G}
using the very same pictures as in (
4-12
),
but the boxes represent
the pullbacks of the highest weight projectors
(splitting off the highest weight summands) in tensor space.
Under the appropriate
assumptions on the involved quantum numbers these
projectors exist. Explicitly:

\bullet

In types
B
and
D
one can take e.g.
\tilde{\mathtt{c}}=[2m+1]_{\mathtt{q}}

and
\tilde{\mathtt{a}}=\mathtt{q}^{2m+1}
and the quantum group
for
\mathfrak{so}_{2m+1}
to get a well-defined

\iota^{G}
. To ensure the existence of the idempotent
one takes
m>\tfrac{G-1}{2}
.

\bullet

In type
C
to define
\iota^{G}
one
can take e.g.
\tilde{\mathtt{c}}=-[2m]_{\mathtt{q}}

and
\tilde{\mathtt{a}}=-\mathtt{q}^{-2m}
and the quantum group
for
\mathfrak{sp}_{2m}
, and also
m>G
to ensure the existence of the idempotent.

\bullet

In type
D
choices that work are e.g.
\tilde{\mathtt{c}}=[2m]_{\mathtt{q}}
,

\tilde{\mathtt{a}}=\mathtt{q}^{2m}
and the quantum group
for
\mathfrak{so}_{2m}
, as well as
m>G+1
.

To see this we can use the explicit bounds given in
e.g.
[
AST17
, Theorem 3.17]
.
∎

Remark 5.2

The idempotents used in the proof of

Lemma 5.2
do not satisfy
an easy recursion as the Jones–Wenzl projectors used in
the proof of
Lemma 4.10
.
See however
[
IMO14
]
or
[
LZ15
]

for some work on projectors in Brauer respectively BMW algebras.

As before for the topological handlebody Temperley–Lieb algebra, we
do not know any explicit way to construct admissible parameters.
However, under the assumption that these exists we
conclude this section as follows.

Note that our definition realizes
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})

as a specialization of
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
, which
is not equal to a definition using perfect matchings. So the following
needs admissible parameters but is then immediate from

Section 5A
:

Proposition 5.3

For admissible parameters the handlebody
Brauer algebra
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
can be alternatively
described as the free
\mathbbm{K}
-module spanned by
perfect matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
with multiplication
given by concatenation and circle evaluation.∎

For the cellular structure we fix a sandwich cell datum as in

Section 2D
, and also with a very similar
cellular basis. Let us for brevity just stress the differences.
First, we only consider positive lifts and we let

\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+}
denote the handlebody braid monoid, i.e.

Section 3A

using only positive coils and positive crossings (
5-3
)
for the definition.

Note that there is a map

\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+}\to\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

that sends positive coils to
positive coils and positive crossings to positive crossings.
We let
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+}
with the monoid basis as the sandwiched basis.
We then get

(5-4)

\displaystyle\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,D,U\in M_{\lambda},b\in\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}\}

as before, with the
D
and
U
part being as for the
handlebody Temperley–Lieb algebra, cf. (
4-5
),
namely only caps respectively caps are allowed to wind around the cores.
The picture is

\displaystyle\scalebox{0.85}{$\hbox to133.54pt{\vbox to105.84pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 17.22638pt\lower-117.06152pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}

The antiinvolution
({}_{-})^{\star}\colon\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})\to\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

is defined as for
\mathrm{TL}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})

with the addition that it maps positive crossings to
positive crossings.

Proposition 5.4

For any admissible parameters, the above defines an involutive sandwich
cell datum for the algebra
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
.

Proof.

The only claim which is not immediate by construction is
that (
5-4
) is a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis, which
follows from
Section 5A
.
∎

Not surprisingly, the cell
structure is, mutatis mutandis, as in
Section 2D
.
The next theorem is
clear by the previous discussions.

Theorem 5.5

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field, and choose admissible parameters.

(a)

If
\mathtt{c}\neq 0
, or
\mathtt{c}=0
and
\lambda\neq 0
is odd,
then all
\lambda\in\Lambda
are apexes. In the remaining case,

\mathtt{c}=0
and
\lambda=0
(this only happens if
n
is even), all
\lambda\in\Lambda-\{0\}
are apexes, but
\lambda=0
is not an apex.

(b)

The simple
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

are parameterized by simple modules of
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+}
.

(c)

The simple
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
can be constructed as
the simple heads of

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+}}^{\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})}(K)
,
where
K
runs over (equivalence classes of)
simple
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+}
-modules.

Proof.

No difference to the Brauer case in
Theorem 2.9
.
∎

Example 5.5

Let us comment on the parametrization given by

Theorem 5.5
:

(a)

For
g=0
the algebras
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{0,\lambda}^{+}

are Hecke algebras associated to Coxeter type

A_{\lambda-1}
, so we get the same classification
as in
Theorem 2.9
, but for the BMW algebra.
This was of course known, see e.g.
[
Xi00
, Corollary 3.14]
.

(b)

For
g=1
the algebras
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{1,\lambda}^{+}

are extended affine Hecke algebras associated to Coxeter type

A_{\lambda-1}
.

spanned by all elements containing only positive coils.

We call the relations collected in

5.6

blob sliding relations
. Because of
their slightly distorted topology, we introduce
cyclotomic handlebody Brauer algebra
before their BMW counterparts.

\mathtt{q}=\mathtt{a}=1
.

In the following lemma we
collect some relations that are handy in the Brauer case.
In particular, up to (
4-15
), these
Brauer blobs

move freely along strands, cf. (
5-6
)
and (
5-7
).

additionally to (

Proof.

The relation (
5-5
)
specializes to (
5-6
), which we then use to
derive (
5-7
) from (
4-16
).
∎

Fix cyclotomic parameters

\boldsymbol{b}=(\mathtt{b}_{u,i})\in\mathbbm{K}^{d_{1}+\text{...}+d_{g}}
, a
degree vector
\boldsymbol{d}=(\mathtt{d}_{u})\in\mathbb{N}^{g}
. Moreover,
let
\mathrm{Br}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
denote
the subalgebra of
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
with only
positive coils.

Definition 5.7

We let the
cyclotomic handlebody Brauer algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
be
the quotient of
\mathrm{Br}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})

by the two-sided ideal generated by the
cyclotomic relations

(5-8)

\displaystyle(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,1})\varpi_{1}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,2})\varpi_{2}\text{...}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,\mathtt{d}_{u}-1})\varpi_{d_{u}-1}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,\mathtt{d}_{u}})=0,

where
\varpi_{j}
is any finite (potentially empty)
expression not involving
b_{u}
such that all

b_{u}
in (
5-8
) are on the same strand.

Remark 5.7

Note that the skein relation (
5-1
) and also
(
4-15
) imply compatibility
conditions between parameters. See
Section 5B
,
Lemma 5.9
and
Proposition 5.10
below.

We consider
clapped, blobbed perfect matchings of
2n

points of genus
g
which we need
for counting purposes.
We assume that these perfect
matchings points are clapped, similar to the crossingless
matchings in the proof of

Proposition 4.6
.
Strands can carry blobs that move
freely on the strand they belong but are not allowed
to pass each other. In particular, there is no condition
on being reachable from the left.
This implies that
each strand with blobs defines a word in
the free monoid
\mathrm{F}_{g}^{+}\cong\mathrm{Br}^{+}_{g,1}(\boldsymbol{c})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Br}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
.

Note that we consider them as perfect matchings, so
there is an ambiguity in how to illustrate
these without further conditions. This problem is
however resolved by demanding that each matched pair
is connected by a cup with exactly one Morse point, and there is
a minimal number of intersection between the cups.
Here is an example:

This operation can described rigorously:
If we label the boundary
points
1,\text{...},2n
, then
the set of perfect matchings is in
bijection with the set of all
unordered
n
-tuples of pairs

\{(i_{1},j_{1}),\text{...},(i_{n},j_{n})\}
that can be formed from the
2n

distinct elements of
\{1,\text{...},2n\}
with
i_{k}<j_{k}
. Each such pair corresponds to a strand in the diagrammatics.
A blob on the strand
(i,j)
is to be slid to the
left if
j\leq n
, to the right if
n\leq i

and left untouched otherwise in the unclapping process.

The next lemma follows from this discussion.

Lemma 5.8

The algebra

\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})

has a
\mathbbm{K}
-spanning set in bijection with clapped, blobbed
perfect matchings of
2n
points of genus

g
where each strand has at
most
\mathtt{d}_{u}-1
blobs of the corresponding type.

Proof.

The above defines a
\mathbbm{K}
-module map from
the free
\mathbbm{K}
-module spanned by all
clapped, blobbed perfect matchings to

\mathrm{Br}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
. On the other hand, each diagram of

\mathrm{Br}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})
defines a
clapped, blobbed perfect
matching by clapping and then arranging the result until it is of the required form.
These are inverse
procedures and so the
\mathbbm{K}
-module

\mathrm{Br}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c})

is contained in the free

\mathbbm{K}
-module spanned by all
clapped, blobbed perfect matchings.
The cyclotomic condition then gets rid of
having too many blobs on strands.
∎

Definition 5.8

We call parameters
(\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c})
such that the
\mathbbm{K}
-spanning set
in
Lemma 5.8
is a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis
admissible
.

We do not know any representation theoretical space
where
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
acts on,
so we can not copy the arguments from e.g. the proof of
Lemma 4.10
. We rather do the following
(which includes the cases where the parameters are generic):

Lemma 5.9

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field and let

\mathbbm{L}
be a field extension of
\mathbbm{K}

of degree
[\mathbbm{L}:\mathbbm{K}]\gg 1
.
For each choice of
\boldsymbol{d}
and
\boldsymbol{b}

there exist
\boldsymbol{c}
and
\boldsymbol{b}
with entries in
in
\mathbbm{L}
such that
(\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c})
is admissible.

Proof.

The same arguments as in
[
GHM11
]

prove that admissibility is equivalent to
the left
and right
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
-modules

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}&\text{...}\\
\raisebox{-1.42271pt}{\rotatebox{90.0}{\text{...}}}&\raisebox{4.97931pt}{\rotatebox{-45.0}{\text{...}}}&\raisebox{4.97931pt}{\rotatebox{-45.0}{\text{...}}}&\raisebox{4.97931pt}{\rotatebox{-45.0}{\text{...}}}&\raisebox{4.97931pt}{\rotatebox{-45.0}{\text{...}}}\end{pmatrix}

is non-degenerate, i.e. of rank
\mathtt{BN}_{1,\boldsymbol{d}}
.
Note that each row contains a unique
combination of
\mathtt{b}_{i}
and
\mathtt{c}_{j}
. Thus,
choosing them all such that they do not satisfy
any polynomial equation of low order ensures
that the determinant of
P
is non-zero.
∎

Remark 5.9

For
g=1
there is such an effective
criterion to get admissible parameters, see

[
GHM11
, Theorem 3.2]
,

[
WY11
]
. It would be interesting
to have such a criterion for
g>1
.

The key players to calculate

\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})

are again the blob numbers
\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}

defined in (
4-9
):

Proposition 5.10

For admissible parameters we have

(5-9)

\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})=(\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}})^{n}(2n-1)!!.

Moreover, for admissible parameters, the cyclotomic handlebody
Brauer algebra
\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
can be alternatively
described as the free
\mathbbm{K}
-module spanned by
perfect matchings of
2n
points of genus
g
with multiplication
given by concatenation and circle evaluation modulo the cyclotomic
condition.

Proof.

By
Lemma 4.5
, the number of ways to put blobs
on a single strand is
\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}
. Hence,
the number of ways to put these on
n
strands is

(\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}})^{n}
. Since there are
(2n-1)!!
corresponding
perfect matchings all having
n
strands,
the dimension formula follows from
Lemma 5.8
.
∎

Example 5.10

For
g=0
(
5-9
) is the dimension
of the Brauer algebra. For
g=1
(
5-9
)
is the formula in e.g.
[
HO01b
, Section 11]
or

[
Yu08
, Theorem 4.11]
.

Remark 5.10

Note also the difference of our construction to

[
HO01b
]
or

[
Yu08
]
: we define

\mathrm{Br}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c})
as a tangle algebra
to begin with, while those papers
start with an algebraic formulation and
then prove that they have the suggestive diagrammatic presentation.

We keep the cyclotomic parameters
\boldsymbol{b}

and degree vector
\boldsymbol{d}
as before.
We are now going to define cyclotomic handlebody BMW algebras,
where we as before use the corresponding positive monoid

\mathrm{BMW}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
.

Definition 5.10

We let the
cyclotomic handlebody BMW algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
be
the quotient of
\mathrm{BMW}^{+}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

by the two-sided ideal generated by the
cyclotomic relations

(5-10)

\displaystyle(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,1})\varpi_{1}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,2})\varpi_{2}\text{...}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,\mathtt{d}_{u}-1})\varpi_{d_{u}-1}(b_{u}-\mathtt{b}_{u,\mathtt{d}_{u}})=0,

where
\varpi_{j}
is any finite (potentially empty)
expression not involving
b_{u}
such that all

b_{u}
in (
5-10
) are on the same strand.

Remark 5.10

Cyclotomic versions of BMW and Brauer algebras have appeared in the literature:

(a)

For
g=0
they are of course just the BMW respectively
Brauer algebra.

(b)

For
g=1
the definition goes back to

[
HO01b
]
.

Lemma 5.11

For an admissible choice of parameters, the algebra

\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

has a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis in bijection with clapped, blobbed
perfect matchings of

2n
points of genus

g
where each strand has at
most
\mathtt{d}_{u}
blobs of the corresponding type.

In particular, the dimension of
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})

is also given by the formula in (
5-9
), namely
it is
\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})=(\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}})^{n}(2n-1)!!
.

Proof.

By the procedure described in

Lemma 5.8
we see that the
corresponding images in

\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
are
linearly independent since they are so in the Brauer
specialization. To see that these span we use

5.6
.
∎

For the cell structure we now combine
the one from
Section 4B
with the
one from
Section 5A

(in particular, using positive lifts). The two
differences worthwhile spelling out are first
that (
4-15
)
tell us to demand that blobs on caps and cups are
to the right of any of their Morse points.
Let
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+,\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
denote the
blobbed positive braid monoid in
\lambda

strands, i.e. the positive braid monoid with blobs satisfying the relations in

5.6

and (
5-10
). As usual we fix the monoid element basis as our sandwiched basis.
Because of these relations
we need to choose an order of blobs and crossings. We choose
to put blobs below all crossings, with blobs on the first strand
below blobs on the second strand etc.
We leave the details to the reader, and rather give an example:

Proposition 5.12

For a choice of admissible parameters
the above defines an involutive sandwich
cell datum for
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
.∎

Theorem 5.13

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field, and choose admissible parameters.

(a)

If
\boldsymbol{c}\neq 0
, or
\boldsymbol{c}=0
and
\lambda\neq 0
is odd,
then all
\lambda\in\Lambda
are apexes. In the remaining case,

\boldsymbol{c}=0
and
\lambda=0
(this only happens if
n
is even), all
\lambda\in\Lambda-\{0\}
are apexes, but
\lambda=0
is not an apex.

(b)

The simple
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

are parameterized by simple modules of
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+,\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
.

(c)

The simple
\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
can be constructed as
the simple heads of

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+,\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\mathrm{BMW}_{g,n}(\boldsymbol{c},\mathtt{q},\mathtt{a})}(K)
,
where
K
runs over (equivalence classes of)
simple
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,\lambda}^{+,\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
-modules.∎

Example 5.13

For
g=0

Theorem 5.13
is,
of course, a BMW version of

Theorem 2.9
. For
g=1
and the Brauer
specialization this recovers

[
BCDV13
, Appendix 6]
, where

\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{1,\lambda}^{+,\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
is a complex reflection
group of type
G(\mathtt{d},1,\lambda)
.
In the semisimple case the parametrization of simples of

\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{1,\lambda}^{+,\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
(and thus, of
\mathrm{Br}_{1,n}(\mathtt{c})
per apex
\lambda
) is given
by
\mathtt{d}
-multipartitions of
\lambda
.

6.
Handlebody Hecke and Ariki–Koike algebras

We define handlebody Hecke algebras as quotients of handlebody braid groups.
All algebras can alternatively be defined as quotients of an appropriate
BMW algebra from
Section 5
.

6A.
Handlebody Hecke algebras

Fix an invertible scalar
\mathtt{q}\in\mathbbm{K}
and recall the definitions regarding
the handlebody braid groups
\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
from
Section 3A
.

Definition 6.0

The
handlebody Hecke algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}

is the algebra whose underlying free
\mathbbm{K}
-module is
spanned by isotopy classes of all handlebody braid diagrams, with multiplication
given by concatenation of diagrams, modulo the
skein relation

(6-1)

Algebraically,

\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
is the quotient
of
\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{B}_{g,n}
by the two-sided ideal generated by the elements

\displaystyle(\beta_{i}+\mathtt{q})(\beta_{i}-\mathtt{q}^{-1}),

for
i=1,\text{...},n-1
.
In this interpretation, we write
H_{i}
for the image of

\beta_{i}
in the quotient, but keep the notation
\tau_{u}
for the others.
In defining
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
we only demand that
the
H_{i}
satisfy a quadratic relation which
is equivalent to either of

\displaystyle H_{i}^{2}=(\mathtt{q}-\mathtt{q}^{-1})H_{i}+1,\quad H_{i}^{-1}=H_{i}-(\mathtt{q}-\mathtt{q}^{-1}).

Note that the coils
\tau_{u}
do not satisfy
a polynomial relation. Hence, as for the handlebody Coxeter group,

\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
does not embed into
a Hecke algebra of type A.

Remark 6.0

With respect to
Section 6A
we note:

(a)

In case
g=0
the algebra
\mathrm{H}_{0,n}
is the type A Hecke algebra.

(b)

For
g=1
the algebra
\mathrm{H}_{1,n}
is the extended affine Hecke algebra of type A.

(c)

The algebra
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}

has been studied in
[
Ba17
]
,
but not much appears to be known.

For all
w\in\mathrm{S}_{n}
we choose a
reduced expression
\underline{w}=s_{i_{k}}\text{...}s_{i_{1}}\in\mathrm{S}_{n}

once and for all. We define
H_{w}=H_{\underline{w}}=H_{i_{k}}\text{...}H_{i_{1}}
.
We still have the Jucys–Murphy elements
L_{u,i}

from (
3-9
), and the analog of
Proposition 3.7
is the following.

Proposition 6.1

The set

\displaystyle\left\{L_{u_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}L_{u_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}H_{w}\,\middle|\,\begin{gathered}w\in\mathrm{S}_{n},m\in\mathbb{N},\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\\
(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{i})\in(\{1,\text{...},g\}\times\{1,\text{...},n\})^{m},i_{1}\leq\text{...}\leq i_{m}\end{gathered}\right\}

is a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis of
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
.

Proposition 6.1
can be seen
as a higher genus version of

[
AK94
, Equation (3.10)]
.

Proof.

That the set in (
6.1
) spans can be proven mutatis mutandis as
in
Lemma 3.6
.
That is, we use the relations in (
3.4
)
together with the following immediate consequences
of (
3.4
) and the skein relation (
6-1
):

\displaystyle\begin{gathered}H_{i-1}L_{u,i}=L_{u,i-1}H_{i-1}-(\mathtt{q}-\mathtt{q}^{-1})L_{u,i},\quad H_{i}^{-1}L_{u,i}=L_{u,i+1}H_{i}^{-1}+(\mathtt{q}-\mathtt{q}^{-1})L_{u,i},\\
H_{i-1}^{-1}L_{u,i}^{-1}=L_{u,i-1}^{-1}H_{i-1}^{-1}+(\mathtt{q}-\mathtt{q}^{-1})L_{u,i}^{-1},\quad H_{i}L_{u,i}^{-1}=L_{u,i+1}^{-1}H_{i}-(\mathtt{q}-\mathtt{q}^{-1})L_{u,i}^{-1}.\end{gathered}

Moreover,

Proposition 3.7
shows the elements in (
6.1
) are
linearly independent if
\mathtt{q}=1

(note that the handlebody Coxeter group
\mathrm{W}_{g,n}

can be obtained from
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}

by specializing
\mathtt{q}=1
), which implies that they are linearly independent for generic
\mathtt{q}
.
∎

Combining
Proposition 6.1

with the respective
statement for the handlebody Coxeter
group
Proposition 3.7
we get
the following.

Corollary 6.2

For
\mathtt{q}=1

the map given by

\tau_{u}\mapsto t_{u},H_{i}\mapsto s_{i}

is an isomorphism of
\mathbbm{K}
-algebras
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbbm{K}\mathrm{W}_{g,n}
.

In order to define a sandwich cell datum we first note that
there is an antiinvolution
({}_{-})^{\star}

on
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
given by mirroring along a horizontal
axis, but not changing crossings (e.g. positive crossings
as in (
5-3
) remain positive).
Moreover, we now recall the
cellular basis of
\mathrm{H}_{0,n}
from
[
Mu95
]
, see also
[
Ma99
, Chapter 3]
.

Remark 6.2

The cellular basis we are going to recall is not the Kazhdan–Lusztig
basis, but the so-called
Murphy basis
or

standard basis
. This basis
has the advantage that it has a known generalization to the case of
g=1
,
see
[
DJM98
]
.
On the other hand, we are not aware of a generalization
of Kazhdan–Lusztig theory to higher genus.

Recall that a
partition

\lambda
of
n
of length

\ell(\lambda)=k
is a non-increasing sequence
\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\text{...}\geq\lambda_{k}>0
of
integers adding up to
|\lambda|=n
.
Associated to
\lambda
is its
Young diagram

[\lambda]

which we will illustrate using the English convention.
Moreover, any filling
T
of
[\lambda]
with non-repeating
numbers from
\{1,\text{...},n\}
is called a
tableaux

of shape
\lambda
. Such a
T
is further
called
standard
if its entries increase along rows and columns.
The
canonical tableaux

T_{c}
is the filling where
the numbers increase
from left to right and top to bottom.

To a standard tableaux
T
of shape
\lambda
we can associate
a down diagram
D

using the classical
permute entries strategy
.
We also need the Young subgroup
\mathrm{S}_{\lambda}^{row}=\prod_{i}\mathrm{S}_{r(i)}

being the row stabilizer of
\lambda
,
i.e.
r(i)
is the length of the
i
th row of
[\lambda]
.
Then let
H_{\lambda}=\prod_{i}(\sum_{w\in\mathrm{S}_{r(i)}}H_{w})

(note that the bracketed terms commute, so
the order is not important)
and let
H_{T}
be the positive braid lifts
of (a choice of)
minimal permutation from
T
to
T_{c}
,
identifying
s_{i}
with the transposition
(i,i+1)
. We then let

D=D(T)=H_{T}
,
U=U(T^{\prime})=D(T^{\prime})^{\star}
and

c_{D,U}^{\lambda}=DH_{\lambda}U
.
Note that the middle
H_{\lambda}
of
c_{D,U}^{\lambda}
is a
quasi-idempotent, i.e.
H_{\lambda}^{2}=rH_{\lambda}
for some
potentially not invertible

r\in\mathbbm{K}
.
Note also that
H_{0,n}
is a subalgebra of
H_{g,n}
,
so we can use the above construction for
H_{g,n}
as well.

Example 6.2

The above is best illustrated in an example. For
\lambda=(4,2)

we have
\mathrm{S}_{\lambda}^{row}=\mathrm{S}_{4}\times\mathrm{S}_{2}
and

H_{\lambda}=(1+H_{1}+\text{...}+H_{w_{0}})(1+H_{5})
, where

w_{0}
is the longest element in
S_{4}
written in terms of the
generators
s_{1}
,
s_{2}
and
s_{3}
. Moreover, for
T

respectively
T^{\prime}
as below
we construct
D=D(T)
respectively
U=D(T^{\prime})^{\star}
by

where we illustrated
H_{\lambda}
as a box.

We let
\Lambda=(\Lambda,\leq_{d})
be the set of all partitions of
n
,
which are ordered by the dominance order
\leq_{d}
(we use the convention
from
[
Ma99
, Section 3.1]
).
The set
M_{\lambda}
is the set of all standard tableaux
of shape
\lambda
.
The middle part is
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}=\mathrm{L}_{g,n}H_{\lambda}
, where
\mathrm{L}_{g,n}

is the subalgebra of
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
spanned
by the Jucys–Murphy elements. The sandwiched basis of

\mathrm{L}_{g,n}H_{\lambda}
that we use is (
6.1
) restricted to
\mathrm{L}_{g,n}
and then composed with
H_{\lambda}
.
We then let
c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}=D(T)bU(T^{\prime})

where
b=b(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{i})
runs over elements
of the form
L_{u_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}L_{u_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}H_{\lambda}
with the
same indices as in (
6.1
). We then get

(6-6)

\displaystyle\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,D,U\in M_{\lambda},b\in\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}\}.

Proposition 6.3

The above defines a sandwich
cell datum for
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
.

Proof.

To argue that (
6-6
) spans

\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
we use
[
Ma99
, Proposition 3.16]
as follows.
Instead of the elements
H_{w}\in\mathrm{H}_{0,n}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{H}_{g,n}
in (
6.1
) we could
also use the Murphy basis
DH_{\lambda}U
(as explained above, i.e.
(
6-6
) for
g=0
). Then, by
(
3.4
) and (
6A
), we can push
the
D
to the left, that is,

\displaystyle L_{u_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}L_{u_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}DH_{\lambda}U=DL_{u_{1},i_{1}^{\prime}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}L_{u_{m},i_{m}^{\prime}}^{a_{m}}H_{\lambda}U+\text{error terms}

which shows that the
c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}
span.
To show that (
6-6
) is a basis we observe that,
left aside error terms, the process of moving
D
to the left
does not change the number
m
,
the powers
\boldsymbol{a}
, and associated cores
\boldsymbol{u}
, while

\boldsymbol{i}
changes, but the property

i_{1}\leq\text{...}\leq i_{m}
is preserved. Hence,
a counting argument ensures that (
6.1
) and
(
6-6
) have the same (finite) size per fixed

(m,\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{u})
,
so (
6-6
) is indeed a basis.

It remains to prove (
2-1
) as all other claimed
properties hold by construction. Let us write

\boldsymbol{L}=L_{u_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}L_{u_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}
for short, omitting the precise indices.
We calculate:

\displaystyle D\boldsymbol{L}H_{\lambda}UD^{\prime}\boldsymbol{L}^{\prime}H_{\mu}U^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{L}^{\dagger}DH_{\lambda}UD^{\prime}H_{\mu}U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{L}^{\prime})^{\dagger}+\text{error terms}

\displaystyle\equiv_{\leq_{\Lambda}}r(U,D^{\prime})\boldsymbol{L}^{\dagger}DH_{\max_{\leq_{d}}(\lambda,\mu)}U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{L}^{\prime})^{\dagger}+\text{error terms}

\displaystyle=D\boldsymbol{L}H_{\max_{\leq_{d}}(\lambda,\mu)}\boldsymbol{L}^{\prime}U^{\prime}+\text{error terms}

\displaystyle=D\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{L}^{\prime})^{\dagger}H_{\max_{\leq_{d}}(\lambda,\mu)}U^{\prime}+\text{error terms}

\displaystyle\equiv_{\leq_{\Lambda}}D\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{L}^{\prime})^{\dagger}H_{\max_{\leq_{d}}(\lambda,\mu)}U^{\prime}=D\boldsymbol{L}F\boldsymbol{L}^{\prime}H_{\max_{\leq_{d}}(\lambda,\mu)}U^{\prime},

where the
\dagger
indicates
a shift of the indices, as before, and
F

is some product of Jucys–Murphy elements.
In this calculation we used
(
3.4
)
and (
6A
) several times and also:
The crucial first congruence
follows from the classical case, see e.g.
[
Ma99
, Theorem 3.20]
.
The final equality reorders the
Jucys–Murphy elements to match the expression in
(
2-1
), while the second congruence uses
the observation that the error terms in (
6A
)
have a lower number of
H_{i}
, so correspond to Young diagrams with shorter rows.
∎

Let
e\in\mathbb{N}
be the smallest number such that

[e]_{\mathtt{q}}=0
, or let
e=\infty
if no such

e
exists. An element
\lambda\in\Lambda
is called

e
-restricted
if
\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{i+1}<e
.

Theorem 6.4

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.

(a)

An element
\lambda\in\Lambda
is an apex
if and only if
\lambda
is
e
-restricted.

(b)

The simple
\mathrm{H}_{n,g}
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

are parameterized by simple modules of
\mathrm{L}_{g,n}H_{\lambda}
.

(c)

The simple
\mathrm{H}_{n,g}
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
can be constructed as
the simple heads of

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathrm{L}_{g,n}H_{\lambda}}^{\mathrm{H}_{n,g}}(K)
,
where
K
runs over (equivalence classes of)
simple
\mathrm{L}_{g,n}H_{\lambda}
-modules.

Proof.

Claims (b) and (c) follow immediately from the abstract theory, as
in the cases discussed before. The statement (a) follows
because whether the form
\phi^{\lambda}
is constant
zero or not can be detected on the component where the Jucys–Murphy
elements are trivial, meaning those
c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}

with
b=H_{\lambda}
.
Hence, the classical theory applies, see e.g.

[
Ma99
, Section 3.4]
.
∎

Example 6.4

The cases
g=0
and
g=1
of
Theorem 6.4

are well-known:

(a)

We have
\mathrm{L}_{0,n}H_{\lambda}=\mathbbm{K}
, so the above
is the classical parametrization
of simple
\mathrm{H}_{0,n}
-modules, see e.g.

[
Ma99
, Section 3.4]
.

(b)

For
g=1

Theorem 6.4

can be matched with e.g.
[
KX12
, Theorem 5.8]
.

(In comparison with

Lemma 4.12
, note the missing cup-cap term.)∎

Of course,
Proposition 6.1

and (
6-7
) give:

Lemma 6.6

The set

\displaystyle\left\{b_{k_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}b_{k_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}H_{w}\,\middle|\,\begin{gathered}w\in\mathrm{S}_{n},m\in\mathbb{N},\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{N}^{m},\\
(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{i})\in(\{1,\text{...},g\}\times\{1,\text{...},n\})^{m},i_{1}\leq\text{...}\leq i_{m}\end{gathered}\right\}

is a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis of
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{+}
.∎

As in the previous sections, we fix cyclotomic parameters

\boldsymbol{b}=(\mathtt{b}_{u,i})\in\mathbbm{K}^{d_{1}+\text{...}+d_{g}}
, and a degree vector

\boldsymbol{d}=(\mathtt{d}_{u})\in\mathbb{N}^{g}
.

Definition 6.6

We define the
cyclotomic handlebody Hecke algebra

(in
n
strands and of genus
g
)

\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
as the
quotient of
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{+}
by the two-sided ideal
generated by the
cyclotomic relations

(6-8)

\displaystyle(b_{u}-\beta_{u,1})\varpi_{1}(b_{u}-\beta_{u,2})\varpi_{2}\text{...}(b_{u}-\beta_{u,d_{u}-1})\varpi_{d_{u-1}}(b_{u}-\beta_{u,d_{u}})=0,

where
\varpi_{i}
is any finite (potentially empty)
word in
b_{v}
for
v\neq u
.

The relations imply that no strand can
carry more than
d_{u}
blobs of type
u
.

Remark 6.6

With respect to
Section 6B
we note:

(a)

In case
g=0
the algebra

\mathrm{H}_{0,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}

is the type A Hecke algebra.

(b)

For
g=1
the algebra
\mathrm{H}_{1,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}

is the Ariki–Koike algebra as defined and studied in e.g.
[
AK94
]
,
[
BM93
]
or
[
Ch87
]
.

(c)

For
g=2
and
d_{1}=d_{2}=2
the algebra

\mathrm{H}_{2,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
can be compared to the two
boundary Hecke algebra as in
[
DR18
]
.

Note also that imposing a single relation involving only
\tau_{g}

(this is the first coil counting from the right, cf. (
3-1
)) gives a handlebody
version of Ariki–Koike algebras.
For
g=2
this case can be interpreted as an extended
affine version of Ariki–Koike algebras.

Our next aim to find a basis
and a dimension formula
for
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
.

Lemma 6.7

If
b_{u,1}
is of
order
d_{u}
, then
b_{u,i}
is also of
order
d_{u}
for all
1\leq i\leq n
.

Proof.

Since the relations in
Lemma 6.5

preserve the number and the type of the blobs involved,
the result follows at once.
∎

Proposition 6.8

The set

\displaystyle\left\{b_{k_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}b_{k_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}H_{w}\,\middle|\,\begin{gathered}w\in\mathrm{S}_{n},m\in\mathbb{N},\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{N}^{m},\\
(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{i})\in(\{1,\text{...},g\}\times\{1,\text{...},n\})^{m},i_{1}\leq\text{...}\leq i_{m},a_{j}<d_{j}\end{gathered}\right\}

is a
\mathbbm{K}
-basis of
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
.

Proof.

That the set spans is a consequence
of
Lemma 6.5
, which we use to pull
blobs to the bottom,
and
Lemma 6.7
, which gives
the restriction
a_{j}<d_{j}
.
Now let
A
be the
\mathbbm{K}
-span of
\{b_{k_{1},i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\text{...}b_{k_{m},i_{m}}^{a_{m}}j\}
with the same indexing sets as in
(
6.8
). Let further

J_{u}\subset\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{+}

the two-sided ideal
generated by all elements having
d_{u}
blobs
on the first strand.
Linear independence follows from

Lemma 6.6

together with the observation that
A\cap J_{u}=\emptyset
.
∎

Recall the blob numbers
\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}
from (
4-9
).

Proposition 6.9

The dimension of the
free
\mathbbm{K}
-module
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
is

\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}=(\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}})^{n}n!.

Proof.

There are
n!
elements
H_{w}
, each one having
n
strands.
Since every strand can carry up
to
\mathtt{BN}_{g,\boldsymbol{d}}
blobs the
claim follows from
Proposition 6.8
.
∎

Remark 6.9

Recall that
\mathtt{BN}_{0,\boldsymbol{d}}=1
and
\mathtt{BN}_{1,\boldsymbol{d}}=\mathtt{d}_{1}
, see

Section 4B
. Thus, we recover the dimensions

\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{H}_{0,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}=n!,\quad\dim_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathrm{H}_{1,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}=\mathtt{d}_{1}^{n}n!,

the former being well-known, of course, the latter
appears in
[
AK94
, (3.10)]
.

To construct a sandwich cell datum one can use the same strategy
as in
Section 6A
.
Keeping the above discussion in mind, e.g.

Proposition 6.8
, the
only difference is that
\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}

is now the algebra obtained by taking the quotient of

\mathrm{L}_{g,n}H_{\lambda}
by (
6-8
).
The sandwiched basis we choose is the restriction of
(
6.8
).
Otherwise nothing changes and we obtain a set

\displaystyle\{c_{D,b,U}^{\lambda}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda,D,U\in M_{\lambda},b\in\mathbb{S}_{\lambda}\},

as well as the two results, where the denote the
aforementioned quotient by
\mathrm{L}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}H_{\lambda}
:

Proposition 6.10

The above defines a sandwich
cell datum for
\mathrm{H}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
.∎

Theorem 6.11

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field.

(a)

A
\lambda\in\Lambda
is an apex
if and only if
\lambda
is
e
-restricted.

(b)

The simple
\mathrm{H}_{n,g}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda

are parameterized by simple modules of
\mathrm{L}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}H_{\lambda}
.

(c)

The simple
\mathrm{H}_{n,g}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}
-modules of
apex
\lambda\in\Lambda
can be constructed as
the simple heads of

\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathrm{L}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}H_{\lambda}}^{\mathrm{H}_{n,g}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}}(K)
,
where
K
runs over (equivalence classes of)
simple
\mathrm{L}_{g,n}^{\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{b}}H_{\lambda}
-modules.∎

Example 6.11

For
g=0
nothing new happens of course
compared to
Theorem 6.4
,
while the
g=1
version of
Theorem 6.11

is a non-explicit version of
[
DJM98
, Theorem 3.30]
.
